items.descriptionOriginal: What's a birthday party without balloons? For Bengaluru-based entrepreneur and mother of two, Sowmya Jagannath, this was a question she found herself thinking about while planning her daughter's birthday. She wanted to try something different, but would her daughter feel that something was missing? Her daughter loves animals, so Sowmya chose colourful fabric decorations in green and earthy shades. Fabric bunting hung across the room, bringing the animal-themed party to life. There were no balloons to inflate or plastic streamers to pull down after the guests left. Instead, the decorations could be packed away and used again at another celebration. The children had fun, and all of Sowmya's initial worries turned out to be unnecessary. Neither her daughter nor the other children missed the balloons. The decorations came from Matter Party, a Bengaluru-based startup that rents out reusable party d cor made from post-consumer textile waste. Founded by Bhavna Kanoria in March 2025, it offers themed fabric decorations that families can rent, return and pass on for another celebration, instead of buying new items that may be discarded after a single use. For Bhavna, the idea began at home, when her own daughter asked for a planet-themed birthday party. The two made buntings from an old sari , finding a way to make the occasion special with fabric they already had. What began with making planet-themed bunting from an old sari for her daughter's birthday eventually inspired Bhavna to start Matter Party in Bengaluru. That small experiment stayed with Bhavna. It would eventually become a business built around a simple question: could celebrations be beautiful, convenient and less wasteful at the same time? How an old sari sparked a business idea Bhavna has a master's degree in English literature, studied interior design and previously worked as a designer. She had also explored ways of making gifting more thoughtful through earlier ventures, including a gift registry service called Giftistree and Scift, a social gifting platform that allowed people to donate to a cause instead of giving physical presents. The idea for Matter Party, however, took time to develop. After making the fabric bunting with her daughter, Bhavna left it on the back burner for a few years. Towards the end of 2024, she returned to it, thinking about how the same principle could work on a larger scale. Matter Party launched in March 2025. Her first rental was for a Lohri celebration rather than a birthday party. The booking came through a friend of a friend, giving her an early opportunity to see how the idea might work beyond her own home. The business now sources post-consumer textile waste through Hasiru Dala, a Bengaluru-based waste management organisation with a textile recovery facility. Bhavna buys discarded fabric by weight, with material sorted by colour, and sends it to a tailoring unit to be stitched into decorations. "I work on the designs and handle much of the finishing myself, including attaching cords by hand. The leftover scraps are returned to the recovery facility," she says. The result is a collection of reusable decorations in around 35 themes, from unicorns and dinosaurs to Superman, Harry Potter, rainbows and rustic-chic themes. Families can mix and match colours to suit their party. Matter Party sources post-consumer textile waste through Hasiru Dala and transforms the discarded fabric into colourful party decorations. Lightweight and fitted with cords at both ends, the pieces can be tied to existing fixtures without complicated installation. Once a party is over, the kit is collected and prepared for its next outing. Bhavna irons the fabric, spot-cleans it with soap and water, replaces cords where needed and checks the decorations before they are rented out again. The aim is to keep the materials in use for as long as possible. For these decorations to make their way into more homes, Bhavna knew she had to make renting them as easy as possible for busy parents. What makes parents choose reusable decorations? When Bhavna began offering reusable party d cor, she realised that leading with sustainability did not always persuade people to try it. "People may not choose it just because it is sustainable," she explains. For many parents, the first questions are more practical: Will the decorations look good? Will they suit the theme? Will they be easy to put up? Will renting them be worth the cost? Each decoration is designed to be used across multiple celebrations, allowing families to rent, return and reuse party d cor instead of buying new ones. That understanding has influenced how she presents Matter Party. She wants families to choose the decorations for their designs, range of choices and convenience, without feeling that they have to compromise on how their child's birthday party looks. The reduced pricing is another part of making the service accessible. The startup currently offers two rental options: a Mini Kit for Rs 1,750, which includes 8-10 buntings and fringes, suited to home parties and smaller venues, and a Party Kit for Rs 3,500, with 16-20 buntings and fringes for larger spaces such as clubhouses and gardens. Both kits also include door or backdrop nets, wreaths and a 'Happy Birthday' banner. A refundable security deposit is charged separately. Customers can book through WhatsApp, choose a kit and arrange for delivery before their event. The decorations are collected after the celebration, so families do not have to find storage space for items they may use only once a year. Bhavna has also tried to make the process of putting up and taking down the decorations simple. The kits arrive ready to use, with cords that can be tied to existing fixtures, and customers can pack them back into the provided bag after the party. Optional party helpers are also available through a service partner for families who need additional support. Sowmya found that the rental model made financial sense, too. When she compared the cost with what she had spent buying decorations separately, she realised how quickly individual purchases could add up. "I had done a calculation of the cost of the balloons and the buntings and all the other stuff that I had bought the previous year, and this was actually cheaper than that. We don't realise because we buy it in parts. One balloon package, one streamer package, then this and that. By the time you add it all up, it actually comes up to the same thing, if not more," she says. From dinosaurs and unicorns to rainbows and Harry Potter, Bhavna's reusable fabric decorations are available in around 35 themes for families to choose from. For Bhavna, this is the kind of shift that could help reusable d cor reach more families: it needs to meet their everyday needs as well as help them reduce waste. 'The children don't miss the balloons' Sowmya has used Matter Party for celebrations built around her children's changing interests. Along with her daughter's animal-themed party, her son has had a Harry Potter-inspired celebration in red and black, and the family has also tried a cricket theme. "The themes will be there, but colours are always the easiest thing to put together in terms of adding that vibe to the party. I love that she has so many different colour options," she says. The designs have also drawn attention from other parents. At her daughter's birthday in September, guests could not stop admiring the d cor. Those conversations have given Sowmya a chance to talk about the idea with other families. An earlier conversation with Bhavna about balloons and the impact they can have on animals had encouraged Sowmya to try celebrating without them. "I was almost scared because I was like, 'Oh my God, if I don't have balloons at the party, how will I manage? Will my daughter be okay?'" she recalls. But the children were happy without them. "Nobody missed the balloon completely. Sometimes you have to take these steps to experience yourself; a balloon is not everything for a party," she says. Shwetha, another Bengaluru-based mother of two girls aged 13 and nine, came to Matter Party for a similar mix of thoughtful design and a more sustainable approach. After every celebration, Bhavna irons and spot-cleans the fabric decorations, replaces cords where needed and prepares the kits for their next rental. "I would try and reuse as much as possible, but having said that, options were limited. So I was very pleased that Bhavna came out with a solution which was a little more comprehensive," she says. Shweta has since used the kits for her daughters' birthdays, including garden and rainbow themes. She likes the range of choices and the convenience of having the d cor delivered and collected. A small placard explaining that the decorations are sustainable also gives guests a way to understand the idea. "Keeping sustainability aside, the design is impeccable. She's thought of various options that you would want to host a party. It's definitely something that people should go for even keeping sustainability outside of it," Shweta says. For Bhavna, feedback like this reinforces the importance of making reusable d cor attractive and practical in its own right. Over 100 kg of fabric gets a second life Since its launch, Matter Party has upcycled more than 100 kg of post-consumer textile waste and catered to 64 parties and events. For now, the startup operates only in Bengaluru. Bhavna is mindful of the emissions involved in transporting the kits over long distances and does not want expansion to undermine the purpose of the business. She is also exploring collaborations with party venues, caf s, restaurants and other vendors, along with workshops in schools that could help children understand how celebrations can generate less waste. The business has grown through repeat customers and word of mouth, but Bhavna knows that making sustainable choices commonplace will take more than one rental service. It also means helping families see that they do not have to give up the excitement or personal touches that make a birthday special. That change can extend beyond the decorations. Sowmya, for instance, has given plants as return gifts at her daughter's birthday and has chosen plantable pencils and stationery on another occasion. Bengaluru mother Sowmya Jagannath chose Matter Party's reusable fabric decorations for her daughter's animal-themed birthday, celebrating without balloons. Shweta says using the kits has made her think about what else she might change when planning an event. Bhavna has noticed a similar openness among children in her own family. Her niece and nephew, aged three and six, have started telling their friends to avoid waste. For her, it is a reminder that children can adapt to different ways of celebrating, particularly when those choices are part of the experience from the beginning. Helping families celebrate with less waste Bhavna hopes to grow Matter Party without losing sight of what made her start it: the possibility of making a familiar part of family life less wasteful, without making it less joyful. She does not expect parents to change every habit at once. Choosing reusable decorations, skipping balloons or rethinking return gifts can be a starting point. "The aim is to make these options feel normal rather than like an extra effort reserved for particularly environmentally conscious families," she adds. Since launching in March 2025, Matter Party has upcycled over 100 kg of textile waste and catered to 64 parties and events. That is also why she wants to expand through local partnerships instead of simply shipping kits across the country. For her, the way the business operates matters as much as the product it offers. A birthday party may last only a few hours, but the decorations can be part of many more celebrations. For Bhavna, that is the possibility she wants more parents to discover: the colourful bunting that made one child's birthday special could bring just as much joy to another child, without either family having to buy everything new. All images courtesy of Bhavna Kanoria and Sowmya Jagannath

items.descriptionOriginal: When the Delhi house where artist Sumakshi Singh spent her childhood summers was demolished, she found an extraordinary way to bring it back. Using delicate white threads, she recreated its doors, windows, stairs and even its gates. Thousands of kilometres away in Venice, Italy, her childhood home became part of an exhibition that drew around 4.5 lakh visitors. Alongside her work stood a towering bamboo structure inspired by Indian construction sites, a miniature Ladakhi settlement made from discarded egg trays and paper, and sculptures inspired by India's natural landscapes. On 25 November 2026, these creations earned India the Visitors' Lion for Best National Participation at the Venice Biennale, one of the world's biggest international art exhibitions. The award was decided by public vote. The winning exhibition brought together installations made from thread, bamboo, cotton, paper and earth, each telling a different story of India. Photograph: (Instagram/@pibindia) Behind the winning exhibition, titled Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home , are five Indian artists who took inspiration from everyday materials, childhood memories and generations-old traditions to explore something we can all relate to: what it means to call a place home. Here are the five artists and the fascinating stories behind their creations. 1. Sumakshi Singh: A house recreated in thread Artwork: Permanent Address Imagine walking into a house that is no longer there. That is the experience Sumakshi Singh creates with Permanent Address , an intricate, life-size reconstruction of her family home in Delhi. The artist has recreated the house using embroidered thread and water-soluble fabric. Artist Sumakshi Singh recreated her childhood home in Delhi using delicate white threads, preserving memories of a house that no longer exists. Photograph: (Instagram/@ abirpothi ) The house was built in 1951 by Singh's grandparents, who came to India during Partition. It became the venue for family weddings, reunions and childhood sleepovers. It was also where she spent afternoons learning to knit and embroider with her grandmother. Years later, when the house was demolished, the same craft helped her recreate the place she had always called home. 2. Asim Waqif: Bamboo that tells a story of changing cities Artwork: Chaal Using 12 tonnes of bamboo sourced largely from Assam and West Bengal, artist and architect Asim Waqif built a 30-foot-high structure in Venice without using a single nut or bolt. The bamboo pieces are bent and tied together, forming a structure that resembles the scaffolding that supports buildings across Indian cities. Made using 12 tonnes of bamboo sourced largely from Assam and West Bengal, Asim Waqif's installation highlights traditional building materials and craftsmanship. Photograph: (Instagram/ @indiainvenice ) The choice of material is central to the artwork. Bamboo has long been used in traditional construction, but modern building practices increasingly favour materials such as steel and aluminium. Waqif's installation draws attention to this shift and the risk of losing traditional skills, such as bending and tying bamboo to build scaffolding. 3. Ranjani Shettar: A garden suspended in the air Artwork: Under the Same Sky In contrast to Waqif's towering structure, Ranjani Shettar's installation feels like stepping into a floating garden. Inspired by flowers and natural growth, Under the Same Sky features sculptural forms suspended from the ceiling. Shettar created the flower-like sculptures using handwoven cotton fabric, steel and lacquer. Ranjani Shettar's Under the Same Sky transforms handwoven cotton fabric, steel and lacquer into flower-like sculptures suspended in the air. Photograph: (Instagram/ @pibindia ) Working from her studio near Sagara in Karnataka, Shettar has used these materials for nearly two decades. Her installation allows visitors to experience the garden from within. 4. Skarma Sonam Tashi: Bringing Ladakh's homes to Venice Artwork: Echoes of Home What does a traditional Ladakhi settlement look like when recreated thousands of kilometres away? Artist Skarma Sonam Tashi offers an answer through Echoes of Home , an installation inspired by the architecture and landscape of Ladakh. Using papier-m ch , cardboard, egg trays and old paper, he creates a miniature settlement that evokes the region's traditional homes, built using earth, stone and timber. Inspired by Ladakh's traditional architecture, Skarma Sonam Tashi's Echoes of Home recreates a miniature settlement using discarded egg trays, cardboard, papier-m ch and old paper. Photograph: (Instagram/ @pibindia ) Growing up in Ladakh, Tashi was familiar with traditional homes built using locally available earth, stone and timber. Designed for the region's harsh climate, these houses help keep families warm during winter and cool during summer. As concrete and steel buildings increasingly replace traditional homes, his artwork draws attention to generations of knowledge that Ladakh risks losing. 5. Alwar Balasubramaniam: When nature becomes the artist Artworks: Drift and Not Just for Us Sometimes, the most compelling artwork is made from something as familiar as the ground beneath our feet. For these works, artist Alwar Balasubramaniam, also known as Bala, uses clay and soil sourced from rural Tamil Nadu to create sculptural panels. The surfaces are marked by natural cracks and fissures, capturing the effects of time and environmental forces. Rather than smoothing over these imperfections, the artist makes them the focus of the work. Alwar Balasubramaniam's Drift and Not Just for Us use Tamil Nadu soil to capture nature's marks and patterns. Photograph: ( Indian Pavillion ) While the artwork was being created, peacocks, monkeys and snakes passed through the work in progress, leaving their marks on it. It is a reminder of the idea behind his work: the earth is home to every living creature. Five artists, one idea of home India returned to the Venice Biennale after seven years with an exhibition built around materials familiar to millions of Indians: bamboo, thread, cotton, paper and earth. Through their creations, the five artists brought stories of Partition, traditional architecture, family memories, craftsmanship and India's changing landscapes to an international audience. The exhibition celebrated India's diverse artistic traditions, bringing stories of memory, nature and heritage to a global audience. Photograph: (Instagram/ @pibindia ) With around 4.5 lakh visitors and an award decided by the public, their exhibition showed how stories rooted in everyday Indian life could resonate with people across the world. Sources: India in Venice 'An Indian postcard from Venice: Why a pavilion at 'Olympics of the art world' matters' by Trisha Mukherjee & Divya A for The Indian Express, Published on 23 September 2026. 'India wins the Visitors' Lion for Best National Participation at the 61st Venice Art Biennale' by Press Information Bureau

Ωστόσο, μια νέα μελέτη προειδοποιεί ότι η αντιμετώπιση της μοναξιάς ως ιατρικής κατάστασης θα μπορούσε να αποσπάσει την προσοχή από τις βαθύτερες κοινωνικές αιτίες της. Ενώ οι επαγγελματίες υγείας μπορούν να προσφέρουν υποστήριξη, οι μόνιμες λύσεις μπορεί να απαιτούν την ανοικοδόμηση των κοινοτήτων…
items.descriptionOriginal: Loneliness can be surprisingly deadly, with previous research linking it to a roughly 30% increase in the risk of premature death. However, a new study warns that treating loneliness as a medical condition could distract from its deeper social causes. While healthcare professionals can offer support, lasting solutions may require rebuilding communities and fundamentally changing the way people live and work.

items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have solved the mystery of strange trenches scattered across Australia’s vast Nullarbor Plain, revealing an extensive hidden world beneath the surface. These subtle landscape features are created as deeply buried cave systems slowly collapse upward over millions of years. The discovery could help researchers locate unexplored caves containing ancient environmental records and unusual life forms.

items.descriptionOriginal: Imagine walking through a forest in the Eastern Himalayas after sunset. The ground is damp, fallen leaves gather beneath towering trees, and the sounds of insects fill the night air. Somewhere among the undergrowth, a tiny frog sits almost unnoticed, blending into its surroundings. In forests like these, some of nature's most fascinating discoveries are easy to miss. And a recent scientific study has brought five such hidden inhabitants into the spotlight. Researchers from the University of Delhi and Harvard University have identified five previously unknown species of horned frogs in Arunachal Pradesh, following five years of fieldwork in the Eastern Himalayas. The discovery has also revealed something unusual about one of them: it feeds on land snails, making it the first known snail-eating frog recorded in India. The research offers a fascinating glimpse into the biodiversity that India's forests continue to hold. Meet the five newly discovered frogs All five species belong to the genus Jingophrys , commonly known as diminutive horned frogs. These tiny to medium-sized amphibians are distinguished by horn-like projections of skin around their eyes, which give them their distinctive appearance. The Tanii horned frog (Jingophrys taniitatii) is named after the Tanii tribe of Arunachal Pradesh, incorporating the Apatani word for frogs and toads. Photograph: ( The Times of India ) The five newly identified species are: Tanii horned frog ( Jingophrys taniitatii ): Named after the Tanii tribe of Arunachal Pradesh, the name also incorporates 'tatii', the Apatani word for frogs and toads. Snail-eating horned frog ( Jingophrys tanogogo ): Named after the Apatani word for snails, this species has an especially unusual diet. Siang horned frog ( Jingophrys siangensis ): Named after the Siang region of Arunachal Pradesh, where it was discovered. Hrdy's horned frog ( Jingophrys hrdy ): Named in recognition of a long-time supporter of herpetological research and conservation biology at Harvard University. Wu-Larson's horned frog ( Jingophrys wularsoni ): Also named to recognise supporters of research and conservation at Harvard. The names of three species acknowledge the region's local communities, language and geography, while the other two honour individuals who have supported scientific research. A frog that eats snails, shells and all! Among the five discoveries, Jingophrys tanogogo stands out for its unusual feeding behaviour. While examining the species, researchers used advanced three-dimensional micro-CT imaging to study its internal anatomy. They found entire land snail shells inside the frog's gut. The snail-eating horned frog (Jingophrys tanogogo) is India's first recorded frog species known to consume land snails, shells and all. Photograph: ( Deccan Herald ) This makes it the first known snail-eating frog recorded in India and the first documented instance of snail-eating behaviour in the family Megophryidae. It is a remarkable finding because it expands what scientists know about the feeding habits of this group of amphibians. Five years of research in challenging terrain Identifying these frogs was no easy task. The research team included Sonali Garg, S D Biju, Tage Tajo, Radhakrishna Upadhyaya K, and James Hanken, who carried out extensive explorations across the Eastern Himalayas. The researchers encountered temperatures as low as minus 4 degrees Celsius while navigating the mountainous terrain. Since these frogs are nocturnal, much of the fieldwork involved searching for them at night, often without a place to stay. Researchers used advanced 3D micro-CT imaging to examine the frogs' anatomy, discovering entire land snail shells inside one species' gut. Photograph: ( The Hindu ) Local tribal communities also played an important role, sharing their knowledge of the region and supporting the researchers during their field explorations. Beyond identifying new species, the team used DNA analysis to understand their evolutionary history. Their findings suggest that the diversification of these frogs coincided with the rise of the Himalayan mountain ranges and the intensification of the Asian monsoon millions of years ago. Why these discoveries matter The findings draw attention to the Eastern Himalayas as an important centre of biodiversity and evolution. The number of Jingophrys species recorded in India has increased seven-fold through this research, while the known diversity of the genus worldwide has more than doubled. Yet, there is still much to learn. Some of these frogs are extremely secretive and appear in remote forests only during short breeding seasons. Further research will be needed to understand their ecology, behaviour and conservation needs. The five-year research involved night-time explorations across the challenging terrain of the Eastern Himalayas, with local tribal communities helping researchers navigate the region. Photograph: ( Indian Expresss ) For now, these five discoveries offer a reminder of how much life remains undocumented in India's forests. Sometimes, finding an entirely new species does not require looking beyond a distant wilderness. It simply requires looking a little closer at the world beneath our feet. Sources: 'New frog species found in Arunachal, Keralam scientist part of team' by K S Sreejith for The New Indian Express, Published on 14 November 2026. 'Two-fold hidden diversity of diminutive horned frogs (Megophryinae: Jingophrys) highlights overlooked in situ diversification in the Himalayas' by PUBMED.

items.title: Η παρέλαση της Ημέρας των Ευχαριστιών του Macy κλείνει τα 100: Δείτε τα φετινά 9 νέα μπαλόνια
items.titleOriginal: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Turns 100: See This Year’s 9 New Balloons
items.description: Ο Snoopy - ή θα έπρεπε να πούμε ο Joe Cool - θα γιορτάσει κάτι μεγάλο όταν θα επιπλέει στη Νέα Υόρκη κατά τη διάρκεια της παρέλασης της Ημέρας των Ευχαριστιών του Macy 2026. Το alter ego του χαρακτήρα Peanuts είναι μέρος της 100ης απόδοσης της παρέλασης, η οποία αρχικά ήταν προγραμματισμένη να πραγματοποιηθεί σήμερα, αλλά έχει προγραμματιστεί εκ νέου για το πρωί του Σαββάτου λόγω των έντονων καιρικών συνθηκών…
items.descriptionOriginal: Snoopy — or should we say Joe Cool — will be celebrating something big when he floats through New York City during the 2026 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. The Peanuts character’s alter ego is part of the 100th rendition of the parade, which was originally slated to take place today but has been rescheduled to Saturday morning due to severe weather. “The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” Macy’s said Wednesday, per NBC News . “Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers, and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.” The event began in 1924 and has run annually ever since, except for three years during World War II. Each November, the retail company adds new balloons to its lineup of massive inflatables, a signature feature of the parade almost from the beginning. The first, introduced in 1927, was Felix the Cat, a hit cartoon character from the silent film era . It was designed by Tony Sarg, a puppeteer and illustrator credited with helping turn the parade into the spectacle it is today. George Rinhart—Corbis Historical/Getty Images Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, November 24, 1932. Unlike today, however, the inaugural balloon had to be carried on stilts , as helium wouldn’t be used until the following year. Other aspects also evolved considerably in the ensuing decades, including the long process of bringing a balloon from sketch to showpiece. Artists kick it off with simple drawings, which are then digitally rendered and approved by engineers. Next, a small model is 3D-printed — a physical pattern for the full-scale version that’s made of fabric coated in polyurethane. “[The model] enables us to map out exactly where all of our cuts and all of our seams are going to be,” Will Coss, vice president and head of Macy’s Studios, told Today during a tour of the studio where the balloons are constructed, adding: “Similar to creating a garment for clothing, all of those pieces are the 3D model flattened out.” The final steps are heat-sealing the pieces together, hand-painting the balloon, and adding about 12,000 cubic feet of helium. Just over a century following Felix’s debut, he’s back for this year’s festivities — a decade after his last appearance. He’s joining dozens of other inflatables for a record-breaking 100 in total. Take a look at the nine new balloons created for the centennial celebration. items.title: Οι Portlanders μετατρέπουν το διασωθέν φαγητό σε ποιοτικά γεύματα εστιατορίου
items.titleOriginal: The Portlanders Turning Rescued Food Into Restaurant-Quality Meals
items.description: Είμαι Τρίτη πρωί στις αρχές Οκτωβρίου και ο σεφ Bradley Cohen, 49 ετών, προσπαθεί να αυτοσχεδιάσει ένα γεύμα από ένα τηγάνι ξενοδοχείου γεμάτο με χοιρινά φιλέτα. Βγάζει ένα κλουβί με φρέσκο ​​λάχανο και κολοκυθάκια από το δωμάτιο, σημειώνοντας την ημερομηνία που έφερε (Κυριακή) και λέει ότι πιθανότατα θα ζεματίσει τα λαχανικά. «Το πρόβλημα δεν είναι ότι δεν υπάρχει αρκετό φαγητό - είναι απλώς μέσα…
items.descriptionOriginal: I t’s a Tuesday morning in early October and chef Bradley Cohen, 49, is trying to improvise a meal from a hotel pan full of pork loins. He pulls a crate of fresh kale and zucchini from the walk-in, noting the date it was brought in (Sunday), and says he’ll probably blanch the veggies. “The problem is not that there’s not enough food — it’s just in the wrong places,” he says. Bradley Cohen is among the chefs who turn donated ingredients into restaurant-worthy meals for Urban Gleaners. Credit: Hannah Wallace He checks out the spices and other ingredients that have appeared in the pantry since his last visit to this centrally located kitchen and grows animated when he finds a container of gochujang, a savory-spicy fermented condiment popular in Korean cooking. “I always get excited when I find this because it adds umami,” he says. He decides on the spot that he’ll make a gochujang-veggie bouillon braising sauce for the pork loins. To complete the meal, he’ll make some macaroni, tossed in butter, garlic powder and paprika. This madcap cooking challenge isn’t for Chopped . It’s for a Portland, Oregon-based gleaning organization. Urban Gleaners is a 20-year-old nonprofit that rescues food before it goes into the waste stream — and helps feed hungry Portlanders. Gleaning, the practice of collecting leftover crops from farmers’ fields or orchards, is nothing new: There are references to gleaning in the Bible, and it was widely employed by the rural poor in the 16th and 17th centuries. And today, there are hundreds of gleaning nonprofits across the U.S. But Urban Gleaners’ cooking program is unique. Helmed by chef Jason Howd, a former pastry chef and caterer who has bee n with the organization for nine years, the cooking program allows part-time chefs like Cohen, a former marketing director, to turn donated ingredients into restaurant-worthy meals. The braised pork, pasta and kale (he ends up sautéing it and tossing in some tomatillo salsa for acid) that Cohen makes today will be refrigerated overnight and packed up the next morning by volunteers, then hand-delivered to shopping-style pantries at local parks, schools and community centers. Perhaps surprisingly, these ingredients aren’t past their sell-by dates. The kale, in particular, looks fresh from the garden. Turns out it was picked two days ago from a nearby farm that sells at the King Farmers Market in Northeast Portland. (Many farms would rather donate surplus fresh organic produce than transport it back to the farm, where they often don’t have storage space.) The pork loins were purchased at a local chef’s supply store. (Donated protein can be hard to come by, so Urban Gleaners has a budget to purchase pork, chicken and other meats.) Delicious prepared meals are just one service Urban Gleaners provides. Haris Kuljančić, the organization’s new executive director, says the need for food has never been greater. The nonprofit delivers about 100,000 pounds of gleaned food per month to roughly 50 locations — including elementary schools, community centers and housing complexes. “We turn it around really quickly,” he says. On this day alone, a Tuesday, the organization will deliver 2,000 pounds of food — mostly gleaned items and prepared food from nearby grocery stores like New Seasons and Zupan’s Market as well as Elephant’s Delicatessen — to a “park market” at Mount Scott Community Center. Urban Gleaners runs three such markets that are open to the public. Urban Gleaners delivers about 100,000 pounds of gleaned food per month to roughly 50 locations. Credit: Hannah Wallace In July 2025, President Trump’s H.R. 1 (aka “the Big Beautiful Bill”) cut SNAP funding — i.e. food stamps — by $186 billion. Tighter eligibility restrictions — such as an 80-hour-a-month work requirement for those under 65 and eliminated benefits for refugees, asylum seekers and houseless folks — have resulted in SNAP participation falling by around 13 percent nationwide , according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities’ SNAP tracker. There are a handful of exemptions (if you’re pregnant, have a child under 14 living with you, or are enrolled in a school or training program, for example) but many SNAP recipients don’t know about these. Another change: H.R. 1 requires that folks reapply for benefits every six months. “They are forcing people to go through the eligibility again, and so if they don’t re-enroll, or don’t jump through all the hoops, you risk losing benefits,” explains Stephanie Barr, executive director of Lift Urban Portland ( Lift UP), a gleaning nonprofit that focuses on feeding neighbors in downtown and Northwest Portland. Needless to say, this can be a challenge for houseless folks (who typically don’t have mailing addresses) and seniors (for whom filling out paperwork can be a burden). In Oregon, these cuts and new restrictions have meant that more than 94,000 Oregonians lost SNAP benefits over the past year, according to the latest data from the Oregon Department of Human Services. This, of course, has led to increased demand at food pantries and the gleaning markets run by Urban Gleaners and others. It’s impossible to fill the void entirely with gleaned food, but Portland area gleaning nonprofits sure are trying. “We hear a lot from the folks we serve about the impacts of SNAP cuts. And the cost of increased food prices,” says Barr, who notes that many of the seniors Lift UP serves are on a fixed income. “Even if you live in affordable housing, your rent can go up. That’s happening in our community.” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Lift UP has a shopping-style food pantry in southwest Portland that serves 17,000 people annually. It also delivers food boxes to 550 residents across 50 low-income housing complexes through its “ Adopt a Building ” program. (Lift UP also sponsors pop-up farmers markets in half of those buildings, so residents can access fresh fruits and vegetables.) Like Urban Gleaners, Lift UP mostly gets donations from grocery stores as well as the Oregon Food Bank, community food drives and bakeries such as Grand Central, which makes a “community loaf” especially for anti-hunger organizations. Still, even with all these gleaned groceries, Barr says that over a third of the people that Lift UP serves via Adopt a Building have had to choose between paying rent and buying food. In September, Urban Gleaners threw a Summer Supper fundraiser for their 20th anniversary. Credit: Leesa Morales In 2024, partly in response to cuts to the USDA’s Local Food Purchasing Assistance grants as well as rising grocery costs, Barr and leaders of other Portland-based gleaning and nutrition organizations came together to form a collective called the Coalition to Advance Food Equity (CAFE). “We really need labor, infrastructure and transportation to maximize the gleaned food,” Barr says. The goal of CAFE is to create a more resilient local food system by maximizing bulk purchasing. Eventually the hope is that CAFE will operate a larger physical food hub that all 14 member organizations can use. (Currently, Lift UP’s warehouse works as a de facto food hub. The nonprofit often takes more food than it can use, so the rest is shared with CAFE partners.) So far, CAFE has done a bulk food purchasing pilot project with Costco as well as with local businesses like Bob’s Red Mill. In October, CAFE also launched a “Farm to Food Assistance” pilot with two local regenerative farms, moving 1,000 pounds of organic produce from Stoneboat Farm and CAMPO (Colaboración Agrícola Mobilizando Poder Orgánico) to partner pantries. This is a mutually beneficial investment: Local farms get much-needed income, and the communities that CAFE members feed get high-quality produce. At Urban Gleaners’ summer fundraiser, there were goats on hand so that diners could hand-feed them corn cobs and leftovers. Credit: Leesa Morales Another CAFE member is the Portland Fruit Tree Project (PFTP), a 20-year-old organization that dispatches volunteers around town to pick fruit from Portlanders’ yards — apples, figs, Asian pears, grapes and more. The harvest is then distributed to food pantries, homeless service organizations and other nonprofits. For its Summer Supper fundraiser, Urban Gleaners asked 15 Portland-area chefs to create dishes from mostly gleaned items. Credit: Leesa Morales Excess fruit gets made into jam, syrup or other products to extend its shelf life. Food preserver is the most popular volunteer position at PFTP. “These volunteers come in and look at what we’ve got, and we kind of decide: Are we going to can it? Are we going to dehydrate it? Are we going to juice it and use it later? Are we just going to prep it for the freezer because we’ve got too much to do right now?” says Executive Director Heather Keisler Fornes. “Yesterday we were making plum syrup that’s delicious and it’s bright pink — so pretty.” Kousa dogwood refrigerator jelly and sea buckthorn jelly were two of the more unusual items volunteers recently made. Some of these are sold at farmers’ markets and craft fairs — which helps spread the word about the Portland Fruit Tree Project. Being part of CAFE has many benefits, says Keisler Fornes. “There are times where one group has too much of something, and it’s so easy to be able to then communicate with the entire group and say, ‘Who wants this?’ Then it’s not a burden to anybody,” she says. The different CAFE members even share staff. Busy season for PFTP is summer and fall. After that, some of Keisler Fornes’s staff work for Lift UP or other nonprofits in the CAFE coalition. I n September, Urban Gleaners threw a Summer Supper fundraiser for their 20th anniversary. They asked 15 Portland-area chefs to accede to a unique challenge: Create a dish out of mostly gleaned items. The inventiveness and talent on display was remarkable. Mika Paredes, chef at French-inspired bistro L’Echelle, made a ratatouille tartine with basil and whipped brie. Ryan Roadhouse, who had just won a James Beard Award for his Japanese omakase menus at Nodoguro, created curried Oregon bay shrimp with cherry tomatoes and spiced seaweed. And Jacob Smutko, one of the chefs at Javelina, a unique restaurant focused on the foods of the Indigenous tribes of the Pacific Northwest, made sumac and corn ribs with sikil pak (a traditional Mayan pepita dip made with cherry tomatoes, poblano peppers, onions, lime and cilantro). Emphasizing Urban Gleaners’ mission to fight food waste, there were goats on hand so that diners could hand-feed them corn cobs and leftovers. It was a uniquely Portland experience — celebrating the city’s vibrant food scene while also highlighting the power of upcycled ingredients and supporting an organization that fights food waste and food insecurity at the same time. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime “No one should have to worry where their next meal is coming from, especially when there’s so much perfectly good food available,” says Gregory Gourdet, chef at Haitian restaurant Kann and an Urban Gleaners board member. “I love that Urban Gleaners puts feeding people at the center of its mission while also addressing food waste. It’s not just about rescuing food; it’s about feeding our neighbors, supporting families, and making sure people in our community don’t go hungry.” The post The Portlanders Turning Rescued Food Into Restaurant-Quality Meals appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.description: Περισσότερα από 400 χρόνια αφότου οι άποικοι πήραν καλαμπόκι, ενόχλησαν τάφους και αντάλλαξαν πυρά με πολεμιστές Nauset κοντά στο Cape Cod της Μασαχουσέτης, 126 στρέμματα αλυκής και προγονικού βιότοπου επιστράφηκαν στην ιθαγενή διαχείριση -- γη που βλέπει στην παραλία όπου έγινε η πρώτη εχθρική συνάντηση. Η Προστασία της Φύσης μετέφερε τ…
items.descriptionOriginal: More than 400 years after colonists took corn, disturbed graves, and exchanged gunfire with Nauset warriors near Cape Cod, Massachusetts, 126 acres of salt marsh and ancestral habitat have been returned to Indigenous stewardship -- land that overlooks the very beach where that first hostile encounter took place. The Nature Conservancy transferred the property to the Native Land Conservancy, an Indigenous-led nonprofit founded by Ramona Peters of the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe, who sees the moment as an opening rather than a closing: "This place holds so many stories that were buried and are ready to be unearthed." The land has been joined to an adjacent parcel now named T8nup hs Uwatuhsh t -- "at the turtle's nest" in the W pan ak language -- where tribal families are invited to forage, fish, hold ceremony, and belong again to a place their ancestors tended for more than 12,000 years. What the transfer quietly insists upon is that history is not only something to be corrected in textbooks; sometimes it can be corrected in deeds. "Returning this land to Indigenous ownership is historical and an act of resilience after four centuries of dispossession," Peters said -- and in that resilience, something older than the wound is still alive.

items.description: Ήταν ο πατέρας που έπαιζε καρόμ με τις κόρες του, άκουγε τις ιστορίες τους στο κολέγιο και ποτέ δεν έφερε το άγχος της δουλειάς στο σπίτι. Αλλά στις 27 Νοεμβρίου 2008, ο Tukaram Omble δεν επέστρεψε ποτέ στο σπίτι. Πρώην στρατιώτης του Ινδικού Στρατού και Βοηθός Υπο-Επιθεωρητή στην Αστυνομία της Βομβάης, ο Όμπλ ήταν σε υπηρεσία κατά τη διάρκεια των τραγικών γεγονότων της 26/11 στη Βομβάη. Εμφάνιση extrao…
items.descriptionOriginal: He was the father who played carrom with his daughters, listened to their college stories and never brought the stress of work home. But on 27 November 2008, Tukaram Omble never returned home. A former Indian Army soldier and Assistant Sub-Inspector with Mumbai Police, Omble was on duty during the tragic events of 26/11 in Mumbai. Displaying extraordinary courage and selflessness, the 54-year-old put his duty above his own life. His bravery played a crucial role in helping Mumbai Police bring a key accused into custody. For his exceptional service and supreme sacrifice, Omble was posthumously awarded the Ashoka Chakra. But for his four daughters, he was much more than a decorated officer. He was their closest companion, their go-to person and the father who always reassured them that everything would be alright. That night, he told his daughter Vaishali not to worry about him. He had always kept his work worries away from home. Even in his final hours, he was trying to protect his family from them. India remembers his courage. His daughters remember the man who made home feel safe. #TukaramOmble #2611MumbaiAttacks #MumbaiPolice #AshokaChakra [Tukaram Omble, Tukaram Omble story, 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks, 26/11 heroes, Mumbai Police heroes, Ashoka Chakra awardee]

items.description: Ένα ψάρι που είχε σχεδόν εξαφανιστεί από τη δεξαμενή Ujani της Μαχαράστρα πριν από δεκαετίες, έχει άλλη μια ευκαιρία να κολυμπήσει στα νερά της. Το Deccan Mahseer, που κάποτε βρισκόταν σε αφθονία στη λεκάνη του ποταμού Bhima, είχε γίνει ολοένα και πιο σπάνιο μέχρι τη δεκαετία του 1990, καθώς η ρύπανση, τα χωροκατακτητικά είδη ψαριών και οι καταστροφικές αλιευτικές πρακτικές επηρέασαν τους ιθαγενείς της δεξαμενής.…
items.descriptionOriginal: A fish that had nearly disappeared from Maharashtra's Ujani Reservoir decades ago is getting another chance to swim in its waters. The Deccan Mahseer, once found in abundance in the Bhima River basin, had become increasingly rare by the 1990s as pollution, invasive fish species and destructive fishing practices took a toll on the reservoir's native aquatic life. Now, in October 2026, the Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS), with support from the Cipla Foundation and Tata Power, released 45 lakh (4.5 million) native fish fingerlings, including 10 lakh Deccan Mahseer (Tor khudree), popularly known as the 'Tiger of the River', alongside more than 21,000 aquatic plants into Maharashtra's Ujani wetland near Bhigwan. According to BNHS, the restoration programme responds to decades of ecological degradation in Ujani, where invasive fish, deteriorating water quality and destructive fishing practices have contributed to the decline of native species. Why did the fish disappear? Ujani Reservoir, formed by the Ujani Dam on the Bhima River, is an important freshwater ecosystem spanning parts of Pune, Solapur and Ahilyanagar districts. Over the years, however, its aquatic biodiversity has come under pressure from invasive fish, pollution and fishing methods that capture even young fish before they can reproduce. According to the BNHS, around 35 native fish species have become locally extinct in the reservoir, while another 40 are at risk of disappearing. According to the BNHS, around 35 native fish species have become locally extinct in the reservoir, while another 40 are at risk of disappearing. Photograph: (Rajeev Raghavan) Invasive species such as suckermouth catfish, tilapia and African catfish have spread through its waters. The BNHS-led restoration programme has also identified the impact of invasive aquatic vegetation , which can obstruct waterways, affect oxygen levels and compete with native plants. The scale of the intervention reflects the extent of the problem. BNHS and local fisheries societies have removed more than 178 tonnes of invasive fish from the reservoir over the past year. Additionally, nearly 6,500 tonnes of invasive vegetation, including water hyacinth, Ipomoea and Prosopis, have been cleared from approximately 2,000 hectares of the catchment area. The October stocking programme included 10 lakh Indian major carps, comprising rohu, catla and mrigal, alongside more than 22 lakh fingerlings of other native species, including kavdas, nukta and bobari. What makes the Deccan Mahseer important? The Deccan Mahseer, also known as the blue-fin mahseer, is a freshwater fish belonging to the carp family. Its historic distribution includes the Krishna River system and its tributaries across parts of Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Telangana. A 2019 scientific review, titled Mahseer (Tor spp.) Fishes of the World: Status, Challenges and Opportunities for Conservation , published in the journal Reviews in Fish Biology and Fisheries, examined the distribution, conservation status and threats facing mahseer species. This is the Deccan Mahseer, revered as Lord Vithoba's beloved "Devmaasa". Found in Indrayani river, it is now endangered due to pollution deadly water hyacinth growth on Anand Doha. A case of authorities' indifference😢 ##goodbadugly #saverivers Image: iNaturalist (1/2) https://t.co/5aTWC0UhK4 — Pune River Revival (@PuneRivers) May 22, 2024 The researchers identified the northern and central Western Ghats, particularly the Krishna River system, as the historical range of the Deccan Mahseer. Its tributaries include the Indrayani, Mula-Mutha, Koyna, Tungabhadra and Panchaganga. The review also highlighted how artificial propagation and large-scale fish stocking since the 1970s expanded the species' distribution beyond its original range. Some introduced populations have even shown invasive characteristics, affecting native fish populations in other river systems. Another study, published in Fisheries Research in 2011, examined the sustainability of Deccan Mahseer fisheries in the Western Ghats using catch data collected with the participation of local fishers. Researchers Rajeev Raghavan, Anvar Ali, Neelesh Dahanukar and Alison Rosser studied six fishing sites and found that catches frequently included immature fish. Their assessment also indicated that exploitation rates exceeded sustainable levels at most of the sites studied. A 10-year plan to bring the fish back The Ujani restoration programme included a dedicated partnership between BNHS and Tata Power for the conservation of the Deccan Mahseer. Under the arrangement, Tata Power has committed to supplying 10 lakh mahseer fingerlings over 10 years. The fish are being bred with support from its facility at Valvan in Lonavala. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BNHS 💚 Wildlife Conservation (@bombaynaturalhistorysociety) According to BNHS's October 2026 conservation newsletter, Dr Unmesh Katwate, head of the BNHS Wetland Eco-Restoration Project, visited the facility on 9 October to assess the available fingerling stock and preparations for their release. The newsletter also records a separate initial release of 8,000 fingerlings near Palasnath Temple in Ujani Reservoir on 22 October. The site was selected after considering its depth, water quality and habitat conditions. The organisation is also working with local fisheries societies and government departments to encourage more sustainable fishing practices. For Ujani, the return of the Deccan Mahseer is therefore part of a larger restoration exercise. Whether the mahseer can establish a self-sustaining population in the reservoir will become clearer through continued monitoring in the coming years. Sources: 'Tata Power Supports Deccan Mahseerconservation Through Long-Term Commitment' : By Bombay Natural History Society Newsletter, Published On October 2026 'BNHS releases 4.5 million native fish, 21,000 aquatic plants at Ujani Wetland to revive biodiversity' : By Mrityunjay Bose, Published on 19 October 2026

items.description: Γνωρίστε τον Divyansh Kacholia του Jaipur, γνωστό και ως DVK The Beatboxer. Μεγάλωσε ακούγοντας Ghoomar και άλλα λαϊκά τραγούδια του Rajasthani. Στα 13, ανακάλυψε το beatboxing και τελικά βρήκε έναν τρόπο να τους φέρει κοντά. Άρχισε μάλιστα να προπονείται για 9-10 ώρες την ημέρα αφού γνώρισε τον πρωταθλητή του beatboxing Skiller. Ο μοναδικός του ήχος τον πήγε στον τελικό του Dil Hai Hin…
items.descriptionOriginal: Meet Jaipur’s Divyansh Kacholia, aka DVK The Beatboxer. He grew up listening to Ghoomar and other Rajasthani folk songs. At 13, he discovered beatboxing and eventually found a way to bring the two together. He even began practising for 9–10 hours a day after meeting beatboxing champion Skiller. His unique sound took him to the finals of Dil Hai Hindustani in 2018. Later, when his teammates couldn’t make it to the India’s Got Talent audition, he teamed up with flautist Manuraj Singh Rajput. The duo went on to win Season 9! In 2023, they took their act to America’s Got Talent: All-Stars, earning a standing ovation. Judge Heidi Klum summed it up as “Bollywood meets Brooklyn”. From folk tunes heard at home to a global stage, Divyansh has stayed true to his sound. Which of their performances would you watch on repeat? Tell us below! 👇 #DivyanshKacholia #DVK #Beatboxing #FolkBeatboxer #AmericasGotTalent #IndiasGotTalent #Rajasthan #IndianTalent #MadeInIndia [America’s Got Talent: All-Stars, Indian Beatboxer]

items.title: Από το πλύσιμο των πιάτων στο τραγούδι για εκατομμύρια: Ο Talwiinder λέει ειλικρινής για το πώς δίδαξε τον εαυτό του μουσική
items.titleOriginal: From Washing Dishes to Singing for Millions: Talwiinder Gets Candid About How He Taught Himself Music
items.description: Τι κάνεις όταν θέλεις να γίνεις μουσικός, αλλά το δοκιμαστήριο σου είναι ένα φαστ φουντ και ο χρόνος εξάσκησής σου ξεκινά αφού φύγει ο τελευταίος πελάτης; Για περισσότερα από τέσσερα χρόνια, η απάντηση του Talwiinder ήταν να τραγουδάει πλένοντας πιάτα και κλείνοντας το Subway. Άρχισε να εργάζεται εκεί στην Τάξη 10, προσαρμόζοντας το riyaaz (μουσική πρακτική) γύρω από την παραγγελία του πελάτη…
items.descriptionOriginal: What do you do when you want to become a musician, but your rehearsal room is a fast-food outlet and your practice time begins after the last customer has left? For more than four years, Talwiinder's answer was to sing while washing dishes and closing Subway. He started working there in Class 10, fitting riyaaz (music practice) around customer orders and closing duties. Without formal music training, he used the time after serving customers to practise his singing. Today, his music has travelled far beyond that counter. 'Pal Pal', made with Afusic and Ali Soomro, caught the attention of British DJ and producer Fred again.., who played the track during a livestream. Talwiinder saw it just like everyone else watching. It was, he says, "a beautiful moment for the South Asian music scene". Between those closing shifts and the livestream were years of teaching himself music, writing songs and continuing to create despite rejection from music labels. From serving customers to writing songs Talwiinder has been singing since he was three or four, but he says the decision to build a life around music came when he began writing songs of his own. Singing was something he loved; songwriting gave that love somewhere to go . The 'Pal Pal' livestream moment connected a Punjabi collaboration with audiences beyond its listening community. Photograph: ( Instagram/@talwiinder ) "The moment I started to write my own songs, I knew I had to release these tracks for people who need it more than me," he tells The Better India . "Once I got into songwriting, I knew this is what I want to do for the rest of my life." There was no ready-made route into the industry. He spent more than four years at Subway, starting in Class 10, and remembers the job fondly for what it taught him about people. "It taught me communication, reading people's energy and having one-on-one conversations with customers to the point where I knew their whole order the moment they stepped in the store," he says. He learnt to run the store by himself. When the rush was over, he had time alone with his thoughts. "That alone time was often used to do riyaaz while cleaning dishes and closing the store," he says. "I loved every bit of that job and never felt like I wanted to quit." His music moves between Punjabi and international listening spaces, opening possibilities for cross-cultural collaboration. Interestingly, someone who once spent hours interacting with customers now prefers to keep conversations brief. He says he prefers texting to phone calls and often avoids conversations because talking for too long tires his throat and voice. He likes to "talk with eyes" and use very few words. He even has a WhatsApp display picture that reads, "Don't call me, text me." Through the songs he writes, however, Talwiinder communicates with millions of listeners. Learning how to express himself through music has involved years of listening to and understanding his own voice. How he taught himself music Without formal music training, Talwiinder learnt by making songs and returning to them. He advises beginners with a laptop or computer to invest in a home-recording setup, which he estimates can cost around $150 to $200, rather than waiting for a professional studio or teacher. "Record yourself as much as you can," he says. "You will understand your voice better. When the time comes and you're in a proper studio with top-notch equipment, you won't be so lost, but excited to go full beast mode." For listeners discovering Punjabi music abroad, Talwiinder offers an entry point into Punjabi sounds. Listening to these recordings helps a singer recognise what needs work and gradually develop a sound of their own. It is something aspiring musicians can begin doing with basic equipment at home. Over time, Talwiinder has also learnt when to stop working on a song and let listeners hear it. He does not believe there is a magical point at which a track becomes perfect. "The song is never ready; there will always be something that can be added or taken out," he says. "You have to trust your gut and give your 100% in stitching the song together, and once it's out, make peace with it and move on to the next song." With every release comes a public tally of streams, views and likes, but Talwiinder says he has never made numbers the measure of his work. He recalls gaining more than four million Instagram followers in a month without paid promotions. He says he has never bought fake views or likes, or followed trends. His focus, he says, is on doing justice to the music, while listeners decide whether to return to it. When he does not feel like starting something new, he returns to his unfinished tracks. "I have way too many unfinished songs," he says. He chooses his favourites and starts finishing them, turning a creative block into a chance to reopen old work. When music labels turned him down The years were not without rejection. Talwiinder remembers approaching labels that did not want to associate with his music. Among the tracks he mentions is 'Khayaal'. The singer's visual aesthetic draws from alternative music culture rather than conventional Punjabi entertainment imagery. "They told me indirectly and did not want to associate with my music," he says. "Funny thing is I still see those labels coming back and asking to work together." He kept making music, including songs that did not immediately find their moment. 'Haseen' was written and recorded in 2019 but released six years later. He says he would not change his older music simply because he has grown as an artist. "I believe good music does not have an expiration date," he says. A song does not lose its value, in his view, because it has been waiting in a folder. With 'Pal Pal', Talwiinder experienced what it was like for his music to reach someone he had not expected. The collaboration with Afusic and Ali Soomro caught the attention of Fred again.. When the British DJ played the track during a livestream, Talwiinder did not hear about it through a label or a carefully arranged announcement. He saw it on the stream, like everybody else. "It caught me by surprise," he says. "It was a beautiful moment for the South Asian music scene." With his signature face paint and unconventional styling, Talwiinder has carved out a recognisable space in contemporary music. Having experienced rejection himself, Talwiinder now wants to help other aspiring musicians find people they can work with. Asked what he would do if a young artist arrived with little money and no industry connections, Talwiinder says he would first listen. If the work felt genuine and original, he would connect the artist with his community and suggest collaborators, giving them somewhere to belong. For someone who spent years practising after work and learning to make music on his own, being able to offer another young artist a place to begin is something he now looks forward to.

items.title: Οι επιστήμονες ανακαλύπτουν μυστηριώδεις λίμνες περισσότερο από ένα μίλι κάτω από την Ερυθρά Θάλασσα

items.descriptionOriginal: More than a mile beneath the surface of the Red Sea, scientists have discovered rare underwater lakes that could reveal secrets about Earth's ancient oceans and the possibility of alien life. Known as brine pools, these extremely salty, oxygen-free environments are surprisingly teeming with microbial life, challenging our understanding of where living organisms can survive.

Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Υπάρχουν λίγα μεγαλύτερα συναισθήματα t…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Mark Schroeder , a professor of philosophy at the USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts, and Sciences, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . There are few greater feelings than the sense of heartfelt gratitude to another human being who has done you a solid. Sincere thanks and reciprocation are part of the glue that binds us in human relationships. But sometimes you’re just not feeling it. You know that you have benefited from what someone has done for you, but you don’t really feel grateful to them for doing it. Most teenagers go through this period with their parents. Maybe you take your partner or colleague for granted. For me, 14 years ago, it was my mother-in-law. She had upended her life to move from South Dakota to California to live with my wife and me to assist with childcare after our daughter was born; no other source of childcare fit with our demanding work schedules and my commute. She made a huge sacrifice that transformed our lives, but there were moments when I really struggled to feel grateful. Since that time, I’ve come to devote much of my research as a philosopher to studying how the way that we interpret each other as people shapes our relationships . That work has helped me to understand why I struggled to be grateful — and taught me a little bit about how to do better. Personal Gratitude I’ve found that the hardest part of feeling grateful to someone is the “to” part. It is one thing to be impersonally grateful that something happened and another thing to be personally grateful to someone for doing it. These are not the same. Both forms of gratitude require seeing something as a benefit. And they both require a humble recognition of how easily things could have been otherwise. When the rain ends a drought, an atheist can feel grateful that the tomatoes will survive. But the atheist isn’t grateful “to” anyone for the rain. AP Photo/Mahesh Kumar A Priests offer prayers to Varuna, the Hindu god of rain, as they stand in the Osman Sagar on the outskirts of Hyderabad, India, on July 16, 2013. Personal gratitude requires more than impersonal gratitude. It is an example of what the philosopher Peter Strawson calls a “participant” attitude : an attitude that we have toward people, but not toward things. And a large theme in my work is that participant attitudes such as gratitude involve giving someone credit for what the attitude responds to. But which benefits we give people credit for is complicated. As philosophers such as Tony Manela have argued, actions motivated primarily by money, self-interest, or insecurity don’t merit personal gratitude , even when they benefit you. Actions motivated by love, generosity, or concern, on the other hand — or other “pro-social” motives — do. Sometimes people fail to feel gratitude because they take someone for granted, not noticing how easily they could have done otherwise. This wasn’t my problem with my mother-in-law. It was obvious that she didn’t have to move across the country to live with us. But it was hard to avoid noticing that she had always wanted to live in California. Sometimes it is hard to feel grateful because of how we interpret someone’s motives. They could have done otherwise, but we don’t think their action was really “about us.” Bad Motives Are Easy to Find Sometimes ungenerous motives can help people to be generous. Your child’s kindergarten teacher isn’t a volunteer. They may be a naturally generous person — but still, they probably wouldn’t be working with your child on spelling, arithmetic, and handling adversity if they weren’t getting a paycheck. It’s still appropriate to be grateful to them. Their financial incentive to show up for work enables their generosity, rather than competing with it. svetikd—E+/Getty Images Your child’s teacher might be generous, but their job enables them to act on that generosity every day. Elementary school teachers are not alone. After all, people’s decisions are often driven by many factors: some that merit gratitude and others that don’t. So if you go looking for selfish motives, you are bound to find some . Take your partner, for example. They do something that benefits you: buying you flowers, filling your tank with gas, or finally taking their turn to wash the dishes. They are partly motivated by generosity, love, or communal spirit. But, as in any close relationship, sometimes they may be hoping to get something out of it : reciprocation, maybe, or getting you off their back. It matters which of these you interpret as their “true” motive: Seeing it one way opens you up to gratitude, while the other precludes it. What Are “True” Motives? The distinction between someone’s “true” motive and the other motives that enable it looks like the distinction between causes and enabling conditions . For example, when you drop a wine glass, the fragility of the glass enables the drop to cause the break, but it isn’t itself a cause of the break — the drop is. In the case of the falling glass, there’s a clear, objective answer to what caused the break and what merely enabled it. But I believe that relating to people is deeply different than understanding physical things. The key question in whether to be grateful to someone isn’t about which motives count as “causes.” It is about which cause we need to bring into focus in order to see the other person more clearly for who they are . See It Their Way In other words, it’s at least partly a matter of perspective. If someone does you a favor, but you know they’re hoping for something in return, you can see that as their “true” motive. But you don’t have to see it that way. Instead, you could see that motive as the condition they need for their generosity to thrive. Shifting perspectives isn’t easy. When you’re doubting someone’s motives , their lack of generosity can feel obvious. But it helps to remember that people tend to believe they’re acting generously . If you want to respond with gratitude, try seeing them as they see themselves. What if that doesn’t work? Well, the next best thing to being grateful to someone is being grateful for them. Starting there is a good way to remind yourself of why you value this relationship in the first place. And it can be enough to simply say “thanks” and mean it. items.descriptionOriginal: A bird following a boat at sea can mean a variety of things to superstitious sailors. They have been seen as harbingers of nearby land, bearers of the souls of the dead or talismans of good luck, among others. Now add this: They deliver data. A group of scientists from the United Kingdom, New Zealand and Spain have wired seabirds with tiny audio recorders and used them as unwitting boat-trackers. The recordings reveal these birds are encountering a lot more vessels on the water than regular vessel-monitoring systems show, according to a paper published today in Science Advances . That insight could help conservationists better protect endangered seabirds from getting killed by fishing nets. “For threatened seabirds,” said Jonathan Rutter , a University of Oxford scientist and the paper’s lead author. “Understanding where they encounter fishing vessels is crucial to protecting them.” Fishing boats can be a magnet for seabirds seeking an easy meal from trapped or discarded fish. But those encounters can prove lethal for animals like the Balearic shearwater , considered Europe’s most endangered seabird . Accidental capture by fishing nets or lines, commonly known as bycatch, is a prime threat to the gull-like brown bird that nests only on Spain’s Balearic Islands in the western Mediterranean Sea. That makes knowing the whereabouts of fishing boats a key part of protecting and recovering such birds. It can help scientist estimate the toll of bycatch, and whether measures such as fishing restrictions are needed. But it’s hard to know how many boats are really on the water. Most large vessels are supposed to carry transponders that continuously signal their location. But there has long been a problem with “invisible” boats, because beacons are turned off or malfunctioning, or sailors eschew the equipment altogether. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , inline-block;height: 100%;width: 54px;margin-left: 10px;position: absolute;bottom:0;right: 0;top: 0;}.IRPP_ruby:after {content: "";display: block;clear: both;} Recommended Reading: The vast ocean is crisscrossed by 1000s of ships that have been virtually invisible. Until now. Some researchers have used satellites to try to solve the problem . But that doesn’t tell scientists how much birds are interacting with these boats. The advent of small, cheap audio recorders and computer programs capable of identifying the acoustic fingerprint of various animals and machines gave Rutter and colleagues another approach. They attached acoustic recorders and tracking devices to seabirds in three different parts of the ocean to see what boats they encountered. In the North Atlantic near the British Isles they used seven northern gannets. In the Mediterranean near the Spanish coast they outfitted four Balearic shearwaters. And in the south Pacific they used a lone Westland petrel. The audio recordings revealed that the birds encountered far more vessels than standard tracking data revealed. The tell-tale drone of ship equipment, compared to vessel tracking records, told the scientists that roughly 57% of the gannets’ ship encounters occurred with vessels that didn’t turn up in normal monitoring systems. For shearwaters, it was around 20%. “We know that seabirds regularly interact with fishing vessels at sea, but what surprised us was just how many of these interactions were missing from conventional tracking records,” said Rutter. The system isn’t perfect. It could be fine-tuned to better distinguish the sounds of fishing boats from other craft. And it wouldn’t work in cases where fishers string lines of hooks stretching dozens of kilometers across the water, far out of earshot of the boat. The method “is not a silver bullet,” the authors write. But it could be “a growing toolbox in which no method provides a complete picture.” So don’t expect flocks of eavesdropping birds to suddenly take to the skies. Then again, these days you never know who’s listening. Rutter et. al. “Unseen but not unheard: Animal-borne audio recorders reveal missing interactions between seabirds and untracked vessels.” Science Advances. Nov. 25, 2026. items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: This week’s episode is a short one with a single theme. Arielle takes a few minutes to thank the people who keep pressing play, wherever they happen to be spending this Thursday, from a crowded family table to a Friendsgiving far from home. Stay for a friendly note about The Optimist Daily’s push to welcome 100 new Emissaries before the year is out. Arielle and Karissa are back with a full roundup next week. If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes Transcript: Arielle: Hi, everyone. It’s Arielle from The Optimist Daily. No full roundup this week. Karissa and I are taking a little breather, but we didn’t want the week to go by without saying hi and saying thank you. In the US, it’s Thanksgiving week. I know a lot of you aren’t in the US and plenty of you might not celebrate it at all. As longtime listeners know, I’m Canadian, and I live in Amsterdam, so this Thursday is a pretty normal day for me, too. But I love the spirit of Thanksgiving, stopping for a moment to notice what’s good in your life and who helped make it that way. And you don’t need a turkey or a long weekend for that. So here’s what we at The Optimist Daily are grateful for this year. You. Every week, we go looking for people fixing things, like the communities restoring rivers, the teenagers creating education programs for their underserved peers locally and globally, and the cities trying something new to make art and books more accessible. Then we get to share those stories with people who want to hear them. That still feels like a gift. Your messages, your emails, the stories you send our way, the fact that you press play, like, follow, and/or subscribe at all, it means a lot to me and Karissa and the rest of our team. I also have one small ask. The Optimist Daily runs on the support of our Emissaries. They’re the readers and listeners who chip in so we can keep doing this without any paywalls and keep good news out there for everyone. Our goal is to welcome one hundred new Emissaries before the end of the year, and we’re just about at the halfway point. If this show has made your week a little lighter or given you something hopeful to bring up at dinner, we’d love for you to be one of those one hundred. As you plan your year-end donations, becoming an Emissary is a lovely way to say thanks back. And with Giving Tuesday coming up next week, we hope you’ll encourage your circle to support The Optimist Daily, too. You can find the link in the show notes. And if that’s not in the cards for you right now, that’s completely okay. Sharing an episode, an article, or a social media post helps at least one more person add something positive to their day, and that little bit of positivity can turn a whole day around. It’s a chain reaction that starts with something so small, and it’s more powerful than it looks. So thank you again for being part of this Optimist movement. However you’re spending this week, whether it’s at a big table full of family, at a Friendsgiving if you’re away from home, curled up for a quiet night in, or if it’s just another Thursday, I hope you get a moment to feel thankful for something. Karissa and I will be back next week with a full roundup. Until then, take care of each other. Bye for now. The post Podcast Transcript Thanksgiving 2026— What we’re most thankful for this year (hint: it’s you!) first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .
