items.descriptionOriginal: Cold floors, chilly corners, and the familiar hunt for a sunny spot in the house are all part of winter. Growing up, many of us watched our grandparents prepare for the season by bringing out thick cotton razais , spreading handwoven durries , and opening curtains to let the afternoon sun in. These simple habits can still help us stay comfortable, reduce electricity bills, and make better use of things we already own. Here are eight traditional and sustainable ways to keep your home warmer this winter without constantly relying on a room heater. 1. Make the most of the winter sun Open curtains and shutters in rooms that receive direct sunlight during the day. Let sunlight fall on floors, walls, and furniture. Once evening approaches, draw the curtains to reduce the chill coming through windows. Cold floors, chilly corners, and the familiar hunt for a sunny spot in the house are all part of winter. Photograph: (Architectural Digest) Thicker curtains can provide an additional layer between the room and cold window panes. This is a humble form of passive solar heating. Traditional homes in our country were often designed around local climates, using natural light, ventilation, and locally available materials. Vernacular architecture in India offers useful examples of how traditional building designs work with natural conditions to create comfortable living spaces. 2. Bring out the traditional razais and quilts A well-filled cotton razai , woollen blanket, or quilt can make a bed comfortable without consuming electricity. Layer a lighter blanket beneath a thicker quilt on particularly cold nights. Keep an additional throw near the sofa for chilly evenings. Instead of replacing bedding every winter, air it on a dry, sunny day and repair loose seams or worn covers. Store it only when completely dry, preferably in a clean cotton bag. Reusing and maintaining bedding helps extend its life and reduces unnecessary purchases. 3. Cover cold floors with durries and rugs Stone and tiled floors can feel particularly cold during winter mornings. Place cotton durries, woollen rugs, or existing carpets in frequently used areas, such as beside the bed, near the sofa, and in a reading corner. Place cotton durries, woollen rugs, or existing carpets in frequently used areas. Photograph: (Amazon.in) You do not need to cover the entire floor. A few strategically placed rugs can make everyday spaces more comfortable. If you already own a handwoven durrie, bring it out instead of purchasing a new synthetic carpet. Shake it outdoors regularly and keep it dry to prevent dampness and unpleasant smells. 4. Layer clothing with natural fabrics A woollen sweater, shawl, socks, and comfortable slippers can make sitting in a chilly room considerably more pleasant. Wear a few layers that can be added or removed as temperatures change. Woollen garments and hand-me-downs can last for several years when cared for properly. If you need something new, consider repairing an old garment or buying a durable piece from a local maker instead of choosing something that may only last one season. 5. Use old fabric to block cold air Cold air can enter through gaps beneath doors and around windows. Instead of buying plastic draught stoppers, repurpose old household textiles. Roll an old towel or stitch leftover cotton fabric into a long cushion and place it beneath doors to limit cold air entering from outside. Check window frames for gaps and use suitable removable sealing strips where necessary. However, avoid blocking ventilation openings, particularly in kitchens and bathrooms, as homes need adequate airflow. 6. Spend more time in one sunny room Rather than trying to keep every room equally warm, arrange your daily activities in the part of the house that receives the most sunlight. If you already own a handwoven durrie, bring it out instead of purchasing a new synthetic carpet. Photograph: (Image generated by AI) Move a chair, work desk, or floor cushion closer to a sunny spot during the day. Close doors to rooms that are not being used, particularly those that remain noticeably colder. This helps you make better use of naturally available warmth without needing additional appliances. 7. Take inspiration from traditional Himalayan homes Traditional homes in colder parts of the country provide useful lessons in sustainable construction. In Himachal Pradesh, Kath-Kuni houses use alternating layers of stone and timber , with thick walls and mud plaster. Their construction helps insulate interiors and retain warmth. The revival of Kath-Kuni architecture in Himachal Pradesh shows how traditional building techniques and locally available materials can preserve architectural knowledge. Similarly, homes in Ladakh have traditionally used mud, stone, willow, and poplar to respond to the region's harsh winters. Traditional building techniques in Ladakh offer examples of how natural materials can be incorporated into contemporary homes. While these construction techniques cannot directly be replicated in apartments, they demonstrate the importance of choosing materials and designs suited to local climates. 8. Keep your home dry and ventilated Damp rooms can feel colder and may encourage mould growth. Dry wet clothes outdoors when the weather permits, wipe condensation from windows, and use kitchen and bathroom exhaust fans when cooking or bathing. A woollen sweater, shawl, socks, and comfortable slippers can make sitting in a chilly room considerably more pleasant. Photograph: (Pexels) Open windows briefly when outdoor conditions are suitable to allow fresh air to circulate. Keeping a home warm should not mean sealing it completely. Adequate ventilation is important for maintaining a healthy indoor environment. A warmer home through mindful choices Keeping your home comfortable during winter does not always require expensive appliances or renovations. Traditional architecture also offers lessons in building homes that respond to their surroundings. By combining these practices with mindful consumption, households can stay comfortable while reducing unnecessary energy use. These measures may not replace safe heating during severe cold , but they can reduce the need to rely on room heaters constantly.

items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. City of tomorrow At first glance, the sky seems to be the limit for Utah City, a new community in one of Utah’s fastest-growing cities, with the developer citing the cost of constructing high rises as the only constraint. The development checks all the boxes for the kind of sustainable, pedestrian-first urban living we often cover at RTBC: high density, walkability, green spaces, convenient transit options. And the project is ambitious , expected to be finished in 15 to 20 years. But Utah City faces heavy scrutiny, as Grist and the Salt Lake Tribune report in a story shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby. Though one new resident describes it as “rad” and “vibey,” members of the local city council call it a “gamble,” expressing skepticism that such a community makes sense in a place full of freeways and single-family homes. As one council member put it: “Walkability I don’t care about. [It] forces a lifestyle the average person isn’t living. Most people drive a car.” Becca says: If you build it, will they come? This is a fascinating look at a dense, transit-centered development that seems great on paper but may not be compatible with local desires. Popularity contest Imagine the U.S. without red states or blue states, just millions of people whose votes all matter equally. That’s what would happen if we got rid of the Electoral College, and according to a New York Times opinion piece shared by Executive Editor Will Doig, thanks to this month’s election, this idea is closer than ever to becoming a reality. Now that Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Nevada and Wisconsin will have Democratic governors and Democratic majorities in their legislatures, those states may sign the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. As its name suggests, the compact would make it so that presidential elections are decided by the popular vote. Eighteen states have already adopted it, and if these five sign, writes Jesse Wegman, senior fellow at the Brennan Center for Justice, “then as early as November 2028 we could experience something no one has ever seen — a presidential election in which all Americans’ votes count equally and the candidate who gets the most votes wins.” Will says: I’d been half-listening to the news about states abandoning the Electoral College, but I hadn’t fully absorbed how profoundly this could impact American democracy — in a good way — until I read this piece . What else we’re reading Himalayan Communities Are Relying on Centuries-Old Water Solutions In the Face of Climate Change — shared by RTBC Founder David Byrne from Time Goats vs. vines: Baby goats devour invasive plants, save native trees in Mecklenburg County — shared by Will Doig from WFAE NYC Citi Bike member rides to be capped at $3.65 after Mamdani inks new deal with Lyft — shared by Rebecca Worby from Gothamist From our readers… Earlier this year, we published a story about wild European bison returning to the Carpathian Mountains of southwestern Romania. This week, we heard from Alex at Live Species , a small independent site that shows the latest published count for each of the world’s rarest wild animals, and those, like bison, whose numbers have recovered enough to tick up past 1,000. “The bison page shows none living free in 1927 and 9,762 in free-living herds in December 2024, a head count from the European Bison Pedigree Book,” writes Alex. “The page also credits WWF-Romania and Rewilding Europe for moving bison into the Țarcu Mountains, where they now range free.” Thanks, Alex! The post What We’re Reading: Building a Walkable City From Scratch appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

Ο προφορικός ιστορικός Ε…
items.descriptionOriginal: When a writer moved to a small Vermont town and began helping elders record their life stories, what emerged was far more than local history -- it was evidence of something science now confirms: that storytelling is, at its core, a biological act of human bonding, one that physically synchronizes the brains of speaker and listener. Oral historian Esther Ehrlich found herself falling in love with every single person she interviewed -- even the medical malpractice insurance executive she'd initially dreaded meeting. She notes that "oral histories, at their most basic, include all the stuff that makes us people, including our desire to be seen, heard, and understood." Holocaust survivor Helen Marks has watched thousands of students be moved in ways no textbook could achieve, and hospice volunteer Neal Allen discovered that helping the dying retrieve long-buried memories wasn't sorrowful work but "quite extraordinary." What sharing stories quietly insists is that every life, told honestly, becomes a gift -- not only to those who receive it, but to the person finally brave enough to offer it.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. What does peace taste like? At the 20th World Summit of Nobel Peace Laureates, held in Rome from December 1 to 4, Miki Kawamura plans to let visitors decide for themselves. PeaceCream, a pop-up she has developed through her Youth Peace Ambassadors program in collaboration with Japan’s Goi Peace Foundation , gives each ice cream flavor a value tied to peace, such as love, hope, gratitude, or compassion. Participants think about what peace means to them, then build their own cup from the flavors and toppings that represent the values they want to bring into the world. “What if we could make peace something people can taste, feel, and share?” Miki asked when she described the idea to The Optimist Daily . The concept is playful, but the conviction behind it runs through everything Miki has built since she was 18. In her view, peace has been left too long to political debates and international institutions. “It should become a part of our everyday lives, something we can experience, practice, and create together,” she said. Youth Peace Ambassadors begins with the individual A boarding school with students from 80 countries Miki graduated in 2025 from UWC ISAK Japan, an international boarding school in rural Japan whose students come from more than 80 countries. Living alongside classmates from so many backgrounds taught her that peace grows less from agreement than from a common aim, a lesson she later laid out in a DailyGood essay titled “I’m 18. Here’s What I’ve Learned About Peace.” As she put it there, “Our differences may sometimes divide us, but a shared desire for peace has the power to bring us back.” From one gap year to more than 100 countries She founded Youth Peace Ambassadors in June 2025, during a gap year that also included an internship at the Goi Peace Foundation , one of Japan’s longest-running peace organizations. The premise is that peace is something each person works on internally before building it with anyone else. Within a year, the network had grown to more than 2,000 members between the ages of 14 and 30, spread across more than 100 countries and connected by that shared aim instead of any political position. Dot Maver, a World Business Academy Fellow who nominated Miki for this series, has watched the approach up close. “Miki has dedicated herself to realizing Peace in herself, and inspiring others to do the same, and then to put Peace in Action in communities around the world,” Maver wrote. “It matters to me as a Peacebuilder who recognizes that peace begins with each one of us.” The Global Youth Peace Journey 1,592 applicants and a three percent acceptance rate In 2026, Miki launched the Peace Journey, a youth peace education program that invites participants to find their own path to peace through their passions, dreams, and fields of interest. It drew 1,592 applications from 104 countries, and only about three percent of applicants were accepted, according to Miki’s DailyGood essay. Maver served as a guide for the cohort. The same year, Miki hosted a Ripples of Peace Retreat in London, presented at the Goi Peace Foundation Forum, and spoke at a Community of Living Ethics Conference in Italy. Maver, who was there, wrote that Miki “touched hearts and minds of all ages” and called her “a living demonstration of peace in action.” Peace Journey 2027 applications open in December The next Peace Journey begins in January 2027, with applications expected to open in early December. What Miki values most about the program is the permission it gives young people to start now. Participants learn, she said, that “they do not need to wait until they have extraordinary resources, influence, or experience to make a difference.” Peace, in her framing, can begin with who you are, how you treat others and what you choose to do today. Youth peacebuilding from Rome to Japan PeaceCream’s international debut The Rome pop-up will be PeaceCream’s first appearance in front of an international audience, at a summit whose 2026 theme centers on artificial intelligence and peace. Miki hopes the experience sparks conversations between strangers and connects people across their differences, using one of the most universally loved foods as an entry point. “Our vision is to make peace not just something we talk about, but something we experience and want to share with others,” she said. Four ambassadors return to the Goi Peace Foundation Closer to home, four Youth Peace Ambassadors will travel to Japan for the Goi Peace Foundation’s annual forum and summit to share the projects they developed during the Peace Journey and compare notes on turning their ideas into action. Miki sees the gathering as a chance to link the ambassadors’ separate initiatives and show more young people that they can lead change themselves. Miki began her undergraduate studies at Minerva University this fall and has brought the network with her, which means Youth Peace Ambassadors now grows alongside a student still working out her own questions about peace in public, much as her essay did. Her aim is to make peace something anyone can take part in, regardless of age, background, or circumstance, and the upcoming Peace Journey is the most direct way to do that. Young readers who want to apply can find the application, once it opens in December, on the Youth Peace Ambassadors website . The post Miki Kawamura: a 19-year-old’s peace network brings ice cream to a Nobel summit first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Οι περισσότεροι επίμονοι λεκέδες στα ρούχα είναι ένα πρόβλημα χημείας και η επιδιόρθωση εξαρτάται από την αντιστοίχιση της θεραπείας με το μόριο. Τα λίπη χρειάζονται ένζυμα που αφομοιώνουν το λίπος, οι φυτικές χρωστικές διασπώνται κάτω από το υπεριώδες φως και η συσσώρευση ορυκτών διαλύεται σε ήπιο οξύ. Λάθος η σύζευξη και ο λεκές μπορεί να σταθεροποιηθεί μόνιμα. Έρικ Τομπ…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most stubborn laundry stains are a chemistry problem, and the fix depends on matching the treatment to the molecule. Fats need fat-digesting enzymes, plant pigments break down under ultraviolet light, and mineral buildup dissolves in mild acid. Get the pairing wrong, and the stain can set permanently. Eric Thompson, a former management consultant near Seattle who moderates the r/laundry forum on Reddit, has seen it happen. “If you pour vinegar on a burrito grease stain on white nylon, you now have orange nylon for eternity,” he said. “Acids bind colour to dye sites on nylon.” His forum, with roughly 995,000 members, has become a clearinghouse for evidence-based fixes, and Thompson’s long technical guides on enzymes and citric acid rinses are among its most cited posts. “I don’t do hacks,” he says. “What I do is: ‘Let’s use biotech and green chemistry and the magic of water and time to gently take care of our clothes.'” The payoff goes beyond clean shirts. Clothes that last longer need replacing less often, which saves money and cuts textile waste. Before trying any of the methods below, check care labels, follow safety instructions on household chemicals, and never combine products without confirming it’s safe. Most of these techniques are designed for cotton and polyester. Enzymes and stubborn laundry stains Lipases for cooking oil Enzymes are the “bio” in biological detergents, and each type targets a different molecule. For grease from cooking oil, the enzyme to look for is lipase, which breaks down fats. Many detergents contain it, though packaging often lists only “enzymes,” so checking the manufacturer’s ingredient information can help. Clare Mahon , a professor of polymer chemistry at Durham University whose lab has partnered with a major detergent maker on laundry research, recommends a pretreatment first: a paste of baking soda and water applied to the oily patch for about an hour. “Fats or oils contain ester linkages and that mixture can hydrolyse those,” she said, meaning the paste breaks the bonds down with water. “Then you get water-soluble products that can then be removed from the fabric.” Speed matters here. Over time, the lipids in oil oxidize and link together in ways baking soda can’t undo, “so the stains can be really persistent,” Mahon said. DNase for gym clothes that won’t stop smelling Workout gear that smells clean out of the wash but sour once it warms up has a nickname online: permastank. The culprit is a buildup of body oils and bacteria. One enzyme rarely found in standard detergents, deoxyribonuclease, or DNase, targets extracellular DNA, a material that has no smell itself but helps glue other grime to fabric. Steve Brown, a product designer in Sydney, ran into the problem with his Brazilian jiujitsu gear before developing a DNase-based booster. “I just couldn’t get the smell out of my rash guards; I had to throw a couple of them out,” he said. Solvents, sunlight and acids Oil-based solvents for bike grease Black grease from a bike chain behaves differently from cooking oil. Mahon suggests spraying it with a light oil-based solvent and leaving it for about 10 minutes before washing. “Because it’s a more oily organic solvent, it can release the residue from the fabric a bit more, then the surfactants are able to lift it up in the wash,” she said. Surfactants are the molecules in detergent that bind to dirt and make it water-soluble, which is why an enzyme stain remover alone can’t replace detergent. Sunlight for tomato sauce Red sauce stains often get their color from lycopene, a pigment whose chemical bonds break down under UV light. After pretreating any grease with dish soap and washing as usual, drying the garment outside can fade lingering orange marks completely, even on an overcast day. Citric acid for armpit stains and rough towels Yellowed, stiff underarm patches come from a combination of sweat and deodorant, and Mahon calls them “a nightmare.” Soaking the area in water and citric acid can help dissolve aluminum deposits left by antiperspirant, though it can take several washes. Oxygen-based stain removers can help too, but leaving them on too long can lighten colored fabric. Citric acid also helps with towels that dry scratchy, especially in homes without a tumble dryer. Stiffness often comes from using too much detergent, hard water, or both. Fabric softener isn’t the answer, since it coats fibers and reduces absorbency. Thompson prefers a rinse with dissolved citric acid in the softener compartment. “I am a huge proponent of using citric acid in the rinse,” he said. It binds to the calcium in hard water and neutralizes the alkaline pH that detergent leaves behind. Shaking towels sharply before hanging them also helps lift the fibers. A repeat cycle for sunscreen Sunscreen stains are among the hardest to shift. Many come from chemical UV filters such as avobenzone, which reacts with metal ions in water that then oxidize into a yellow mark. A rust stain remover can reverse the oxidation, but the metal stays in the fabric, and the stain can return as it dries. Thompson’s approach is a cycle of “pretreating, waiting, washing, rust-removing, and then washing again.” Machine care and the last-resort deep clean Cleaning the washer itself A smelly washing machine will pass its odor on to everything in it. Manufacturers recommend a monthly cleaning cycle on the hottest setting, wiping out the rubber door seal, and periodically emptying and rinsing the drain pump filter, which collects lint, plastic, paper, and residue. Polyquat spots Some mystery marks appear only after washing. These are often polyquat stains, caused by polyquaterniums , polymers found in hair products, contact lens solution and children’s bubble mix. In the wash, they attract dirt and dye to the fabric, which effectively turns that patch into a color-catcher sheet, Mahon explained. Color-remover products can sometimes help, but they don’t work on indigo, so a polyquat spot that picked up dye from jeans is likely permanent. Thompson’s “spa day” For persistent odors and dinginess, Thompson’s forum is known for a long, enzyme-powered soak he calls a spa day. Items soak in water with a measured amount of enzyme detergent, held at around 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) for several hours, before a regular wash; he also adds household ammonia for degreasing. Ammonia must never be mixed with chlorine bleach, since the combination releases a toxic gas. “It’s incumbent on all of us to keep textiles in the productive-use space as long as possible,” Thompson said. “Spa day is the last-ditch effort to do so when previous care has failed.” None of this needs to become a weekly routine. Overwashing wears out fabric, and shorter cycles at lower temperatures use less energy. Thompson calls a regular mixed load “good enough” for most days, and Mahon thinks the bigger risk may be overthinking it. “To be honest with you, most people’s clothes aren’t actually that dirty,” she said. The chemistry becomes useful on the days a favorite shirt seems ruined, when knowing which molecule caused the stain can decide whether it goes back in the drawer or into the trash. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary. items.titleOriginal: Psilocybin and Ketamine Break Rigid Habits to Improve Decision-Making
items.description: Πώς τα ψυχεδελικά βοηθούν τον εγκέφαλο να απελευθερωθεί από εδραιωμένα μοτίβα σκέψης; Μια νέα μελέτη δείχνει ότι τόσο η ψιλοκυβίνη όσο και η κεταμίνη μειώνουν την εξάρτηση από επαναλαμβανόμενες συνήθειες και οξύνουν τη λήψη αποφάσεων που καθοδηγούνται από την αίσθηση, σμιλεύοντας απαλά τη δραστηριότητα του τροχιακού μετωπιαίου φλοιού.
items.descriptionOriginal: How do psychedelics help the brain break free from entrenched patterns of thought? A new study shows that both psilocybin and ketamine reduce reliance on repetitive habits and sharpen sensory-guided decision-making by gently sculpting orbitofrontal cortex activity.

items.description: Ακόμη και οι πιο λεπτομερείς χάρτες καλωδίωσης εγκεφάλου συχνά χάνουν εξαιρετικά λεπτές κυψελοειδείς συνδέσεις. Μια νέα θεραπεία «ένα και τελειωμένο» που επεξεργάζεται τα γονίδια απευθείας μέσα…
items.descriptionOriginal: The one-time treatment, lonvo-z, targets a genetic disorder that triggers painful and potentially dangerous swelling in the throat and elsewhere in the body. Gene editing could cure a host of deadly hereditary diseases, but current approaches are slow, costly, and grueling for patients. A new “one-and-done” therapy that edits genes directly inside the body could change the arithmetic and is on the cusp of approval in the US. Today’s only approved CRISPR treatment, Casgevy, works by extracting a patient’s blood stem cells, sending them away to be edited, and then infusing them back into the body. Each dose has to be made individually, and patients must first go through harsh chemotherapy to make way for the modified cells. Editing cells outside the body has been the established route so far because it sidesteps concerns about off-target edits and the difficulty of delivering the editing machinery to the right place in the body. It also means each treatment is bespoke, dramatically increasing the cost and complications. More recently, researchers have focused on approaches that edit cells inside the body . And now, Intellia Therapeutics has asked the FDA to approve a therapy that edits genes in the liver to treat a rare swelling disorder. The submission is based on promising results that show the treatment worked in patients for four years, according to Nature . The therapy targets a form of hereditary angioedema, a genetic disorder that triggers painful and potentially dangerous bouts of swelling in the throat and elsewhere in the body. Existing drugs can help prevent attacks, but they are only partially effective, access is patchy, and patients have to take them for life. Intellia’s new drug lonvoguran ziclumeran (lonvo-z) uses CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing to switch off the gene that produces prekallikrein, a liver protein that causes blood vessels to leak fluid, leading to swelling in surrounding tissue. But rather than editing cells extracted from the body, the treatment encapsulates mRNA sequences encoding the CRISPR machinery inside tiny fat-based particles. After they’re infused into the blood, these nanoparticles travel to the liver, where prekallikrein is made, and are absorbed by liver cells. Once inside they release their cargo, and each cell reads the mRNA and builds the gene editing machinery itself. The newly constructed gene editor then cuts the cell’s DNA at the target gene, deactivating it. The infusion takes only four hours, so the whole procedure is done in a day. Clinical results so far have been encouraging. In an 80-person trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine in June, 62 percent of those given lonvo-z had no swelling attacks in the six months after treatment, compared with 11 percent of those who received a placebo. The treatment cut attack rates 87 percent overall and moderate or severe attacks 91 percent. The newly released long-term figures pooled participants from several trials, who had averaged more than three attacks a month before treatment. The number of attacks fell to fewer than 0.5 a month afterwards and stayed there for four years, with no serious safety events. “It’s very reassuring,” Jonathan Bernstein, a hereditary-angioedema specialist at the University of Cincinnati in Ohio and an investigator on a lonvo-z trial, told Nature , referring to the four-year results. “That’s what you’re supposed to see.” For patients, Bernstein said, a one-off gene edit could replace a lifetime of managing medications to prevent and treat attacks. And it would avoid many of the hurdles that come with editing cells outside the body. But editing genes inside the body brings a different set of risks. For a start, there is no opportunity to screen out cells in which the CRISPR system has made unwanted edits elsewhere in the genome. Patients could also suffer harmful immune reactions to the treatment. Intellia already had one serious safety scare last year. The FDA put two of the company’s in vivo trials for a different disorder on hold after a participant with other health conditions died following treatment. The episode worries Sandra Christiansen, a hereditary-angioedema researcher and retired clinician at the University of California, San Diego, who told Nature she is uneasy about the unintended consequences of permanently removing a protein the body normally makes. “The question is really: Well, you are doing a permanent intervention, and you’re taking out a normal gene,” she said. “Could that be a problem?” Intellia is not the only group trying to edit genes inside the body though. Eli Lilly is testing a one-shot treatment called VERVE-102 that switches off a cholesterol-related gene in the liver using base editing, a more precise version of CRISPR. And Prime Medicine recently treated the first person in a trial using prime editing to fix a mutation behind Wilson disease , which causes copper to build up in the liver. If the FDA gives the go-ahead, lonvo-z would claim the title of the world’s first CRISPR medicine delivered directly into the body. Whether it lives up to its one-and-done billing, however, will depend on how patients fare in the years that follow. The post FDA Set to Approve First CRISPR Therapy That Edits Genes Inside the Body appeared first on SingularityHub .

items.description: Διαφορετικές οδοί για τις καθαρές μηδενικές εκπομπές αερίων του θερμοκηπίου θα μπορούσαν να έχουν εξαιρετικά διαφορετικές επιπτώσεις σε άλλα μέρη του φυσικού περιβάλλοντος, σύμφωνα με μια νέα μελέτη. «Το πώς θα απελευθερώνουμε τις ανθρακούχες εκπομπές μπορεί να έχει εξίσου σημασία με το πόσο φιλόδοξοι είναι οι κλιματικοί μας στόχοι», λέει το μέλος της ομάδας μελέτης Alvaro Hahn Menacho, υποψήφιος διδάκτορας στο Ινστιτούτο Paul Scherrer (PSI) στο Zur.…
items.descriptionOriginal: Different pathways to net zero greenhouse gas emissions could have wildly different effects on other parts of the natural environment, according to a new study. “How we decarbonize may matter just as much as how ambitious our climate goals are,” says study team member Alvaro Hahn Menacho , a PhD candidate at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Zurich, Switzerland. Until now, most research on net-zero pathways has focused on cost and greenhouse gas emissions. Some studies have looked at the broader environmental context at a national level, but never at a global scale. The new work provides an opportunity to get a clearer picture of the tradeoffs involved before decarbonization infrastructure is locked into place, Hahn Menacho and his colleagues say. The researchers analyzed 24 different climate change mitigation pathways from three existing large-scale modeling efforts. The pathways involve a range of socioeconomic development patterns (for example, will population growth be high, or more modest?), climate ambition ( will the world decarbonize fast, or slowly? ), and energy system specifics (will the green transition involve a lot of wind and solar power, or a lot of bioenergy with carbon capture?). They assessed these scenarios with a life cycle analysis using a new open-source software tool, also developed at PSI, that enabled them to compare the future impact of the pathways on human health, both;} Recommended Reading: The overlooked wiring problem in the clean-energy transition “Decarbonization brings substantial benefits beyond reducing greenhouse gas emissions, particularly for human health and ecosystem quality,” Hahn Menacho says. “However, it does not automatically reduce pressures on natural resources such as land, water, and minerals.” Moving away from fossil fuels could lead to anywhere between a 13% decrease and a 354% increase in land use by the energy system, the researchers found. That’s because this figure strongly depends on the use of biomass. Pathways that rely heavily on bioenergy will require a lot more land to grow biofuel crops. Similarly, a pathway that relies more on carbon capture to soak up ongoing emissions will require a larger energy system and impose higher burdens on various aspects of the environment than one that prioritizes preventing emissions in the first place – even if the result is a similar emissions balance overall. “One particularly interesting finding was that ambitious climate goals primarily accelerate the demand for critical minerals rather than substantially increasing their cumulative extraction over the century,” Hahn Menacho says. Critical minerals are substances like lithium, cobalt, and nickel that are needed for green technologies but involve supply chain risks due to their scarcity or limited distribution. The finding “suggests that delaying decarbonization does not necessarily solve the resource challenge,” he says. The researchers aim to take these global insights and drill back down “to develop more geographically detailed impact assessments,” Hahn Menacho says. Among other research priorities, “an important next step is better understanding where these environmental pressures occur and how they can be mitigated.” Source: Hahn Menacho A. items.descriptionOriginal: In a pocket park wedged between busy Montreal roads, the sound of ocean waves now washes over a neighborhood that has long carried a quiet grief - the displacement of islanders who left the Magdalen Islands generations ago and never quite left them behind. Researchers and artists collaborated to pipe in field recordings of coastal life, not as decoration, but as a form of cultural memory made audible, transforming a space people once moved through into one they now seek out. "Sound is more than just noise, it can be a powerful resource," says McGill professor Catherine Guastavino, whose team helped design the installation - and the results bear that out, with one resident now visiting specifically for "the boost it gives me afterwards." What the project quietly demonstrates is that the antidote to what alienates us in urban life may sometimes be found not in silence, but in the right kind of listening. It turns out that belonging can be transmitted through frequency, and that a community's sense of home need not be lost just because the geography has changed.

Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Κατά τη διάρκεια τεσσάρων ημερών στην Ολυμπιακή Χερσόνησο της Ουάσιγκτον, είδα έναν Ολυμπιακό…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Phil Starks , an associate professor of biology at Tufts University, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . During four days on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula, I saw an Olympic marmot , a species found nowhere else on Earth; four bumblebee species working the same lavender plant; three western hermit crab species new to me; and five orcas slicing through the dark water off Ediz Hook . Any one of them could have been the trip’s highlight. Yet the encounter I cannot stop talking about occurred at low tide at Tongue Point , when I heard a barnacle. While I had seen thousands of barnacles, I had never imagined I could hear one. It made a noise that sounded like: Clickety-clack. Clickety-clack. Pop. As a professor who teaches about animal behavior , I know that the distinction between encountering an animal and actually noticing what it is doing is one of the simplest ways into natural history . It requires no laboratory and, at first, no special expertise. Mostly it requires learning how to let something ordinary become interesting again. At Low Tide My habit in places like a rocky shore is to become still and let my vision soften. Instead of staring at one point, I allow movement anywhere in the visual field to pull my attention. At Tongue Point, I was thinking about the demands of life in the intertidal zone , the shore between high and low tide: temperature swings, desiccation, and the cost of remaining clamped shut in open air. Then I noticed the soundscape. At first, the clicking was just coastal noise. I attributed it to small shore crabs moving among the mussels, or hermit crab shells knocking against them. Then one sharp pop pulled my attention to a single acorn barnacle . Its tiny opening was slightly unsealed, and two small plates were moving against its deeply ridged shell. The movement appeared to coincide with another pop. Then another. The repetition gave me something to follow. You can train yourself to do this almost anywhere. Watch honeybees fly around and see what you notice. When I take students or my sons to watch honeybees , I tell them not to stare directly at the hive entrance. Instead, sit nearby, look toward the open sky, and relax your gaze. At first you see empty air. Then a bee crosses it. Then another. Within moments the emptiness becomes a busy airport of arrivals and departures. Nothing new has entered the scene. You have just changed what you are capable of noticing. A Web of Assumptions Observation has its own traps. Sometimes you can miss behavior because it blends into the background. Other times you see something perfectly but stop asking questions because somebody has already told you what it means. Orb-weaver spiders offer a good example . Some add conspicuous bands or patches of dense silk to their webs. These structures are called stabilimenta , a name inherited from the old idea that they stabilize or strengthen the web. But they don’t. Researchers later found evidence for several possible functions: attracting prey, deterring or confusing predators, protecting webs from larger animals, and, in some cases, helping with temperature regulation. Different functions may matter in different species, environments, or stages of life. Muhammad Mahdi Karim/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA This orb-weaver rests on the stabilimentum of its web. I first became interested in the debate over stabilimentum function because I was unconvinced that one explanation could account for all the evidence. I started out asking whether somebody was wrong. The better question turned out to be why researchers expected one universal answer in the first place. That remains one of my favorite lessons from animal behavior: A name can be useful, but it can also sneak in an explanation. Once you think you know what something is, you become less likely to watch what it actually does. Seeing Isn’t Knowing The opposite mistake is just as easy: seeing something interesting and immediately deciding you understand it. After I returned from the Olympic Peninsula, I emailed a retired marine invertebrate zoologist and described what I had seen and heard. His response was delighted and appropriately skeptical: “Doubt it. Take a short video next time.” Aleria Jensen/NOAA/NMFS/AKFSC via Flickr How would you confirm these barnacles made a sound? I saw an open barnacle move and heard a pop at the same time. That is an observation. I did not demonstrate that the barnacle produced the sound. A mussel bed contains crabs, moving shells, and a host of other possible sources. A close-up video with synchronized audio could test whether the same visible movement repeatedly coincided with each pop. Noticing something is the start of science. It does not let you skip the work that follows. Look Again For anyone who wants to become a better naturalist , a simple sequence helps: Notice something. Describe it carefully. Ask what else could explain it. Decide what evidence would distinguish among those possibilities. Try it somewhere familiar: a backyard, city park, pond edge, patch of flowers, or shoreline. Stay longer than feels necessary. Let the sights and sounds become background. Then look for repetition. One movement, then another like it. One sound that separates from the rest. An animal returning to the same place. And once something catches your attention, resist the urge to explain it too quickly. Watch again. You may discover something genuinely unusual. More likely, you will discover something ordinary that you had never actually seen before. I may not have witnessed rare behavior at Tongue Point or identified a rare species. But I stayed long enough to wonder what I was hearing. Maybe that was rare enough. RELATED: What Are the Mysterious Creatures Quacking Under the Sea? We’re a Step Closer to Finding Out

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Maybe you’ve noticed it creeping in over the last few weeks. You finish lunch, and an hour later you’re already drifting back toward the kitchen. The bowl of soup that would have filled you up in May barely makes a dent, and somewhere around four o’clock you’d trade almost anything for a warm slice of something with cinnamon on top. It’s easy to blame the pumpkin bread and cider doughnuts suddenly everywhere you look, and they’re certainly not helping. But if you’ve been feeling hungrier in the fall, there’s more going on than seasonal temptation. Your body is responding to shorter days, colder air, and some very old instincts, all at the same time. Registered dietitian Lyndsay Hall of JM Nutrition walked through what’s behind that bigger appetite, and the good news is that none of it means you’re doing anything wrong. Why you feel hungrier in the fall Old instincts that haven’t caught up For most of human history, the end of summer meant leaner months were coming. “For those living in colder climates, fall signifies the transition from summer to winter, when historically food access would have been limited in the coming months, so people would eat more and put on some extra weight intentionally to help them get through the cold winter season,” Hall said. Your grocery store stays stocked all year, of course, but your body doesn’t know that. Like animals building up reserves before hibernation, some of that seasonal pull toward eating more may be wiring we’ve carried with us for a very long time. Staying warm takes energy Cold weather asks more of you physically, too. “When we start to feel physically cold, our bodies will expend more energy trying to keep us warm (i.e., by shivering) and diverting more blood flow to organs to keep them up and running,” Hall said. More energy spent means your body sends stronger signals to refuel. Less sunlight, shifting moods Then there’s the light, or the lack of it. “Many people experience a drop in serotonin levels during the fall and winter months due to decreased sun exposure and the cold weather making it difficult to get outside as often as we might during the summer months,” Hall said. Lower serotonin can affect hunger and fullness cues, making cravings stronger and meals feel less satisfying. For some people, the darker months bring more than a mild case of the winter blues . If low mood, fatigue, or changes in appetite start to feel heavy or stick around, it’s a good idea to check in with a doctor, since seasonal affective disorder is common and very treatable. Holidays on the horizon Fall also kicks off the stretch of the year when so many gatherings revolve around food. “Over time, we have created psychological associations between certain times of year and eating more or indulging. Thanksgiving, for example, occurs in the fall months and is often centered around eating that many look forward to,” Hall said. The same goes for Christmas, Hanukkah, Kwanzaa and New Year’s, when the dishes on the table tend to be rich, hearty and tied up with memories. Staying satisfied through fall and winter None of this calls for a diet or a calorie tracker. Hall’s approach is to lean on three things that help meals stick with you longer: protein, fiber, and healthy fats. “Protein and fiber help to keep us physically satiated for longer periods of time,” she said. Together with fats, they slow digestion, so a cozy meal keeps you going well into the afternoon. Fold protein into the comfort foods you love Hall suggests stirring Greek yogurt or cottage cheese, or a high-protein plant-based alternative, into muffin batter, pancakes, and quick breads. A splash of milk or a dairy-free version in your oatmeal or morning latte works the same way. Eggs, tofu, fish and poultry can round out casseroles and pasta bakes, too. Let vegetables and legumes do the heavy lifting Soups, stews and chilis are perfect for this. Skin-on potatoes, winter squash, eggplant, peppers, leafy greens and green beans add fiber without changing the spirit of a dish, and apples or pomegranate seeds bring a bright, seasonal crunch to salads. “Beans, chickpeas and lentils are great ways to add both protein and lots of fiber to soups, stews, chilis and stuffed vegetables,” Hall said. Give seasonal baking a fiber boost Seasonal treats can pull a little more weight, too. “Oat bran, chia, ground flaxseed, grated zucchini or carrot, and dried fruits can be easy sources of extra fiber for any baked good or hot cereals,” Hall said. So the next time your stomach rumbles an hour after lunch on a gray November afternoon, you can take it as your body doing what it’s long been built to do. Answer it with something warm and filling, save room for the dishes that only come around once a year, and let the season be one you enjoy at the table instead of second-guessing every bite. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . Το χάπι του Αλτσχάιμερ, αναπτύξτε…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A once-daily tablet called AR1001 slowed cognitive decline by 31 percent over a year in people with early Alzheimer’s disease who were not on any other Alzheimer’s medication, according to phase 3 results presented at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference in Boston. The Alzheimer’s pill, developed by South Korean company AriBio, belongs to the same drug family as Viagra. Across the full trial population, which included patients already taking other Alzheimer’s drugs, the effect did not reach statistical significance. How the Alzheimer’s pill works A PDE5 inhibitor, not an amyloid drug AR1001 is a phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE5) inhibitor. Drugs in this class relax blood vessels, which is how they work for erectile dysfunction, and for the brain the effect is increased blood flow. Tara Spires-Jones, a professor of neurodegeneration at the University of Edinburgh and a fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences, said the mechanism likely goes beyond circulation. “This drug acts through boosting blood flow and likely also directly stimulating pathways in brain cells that promote learning and memory ,” she said. That sets it apart from the disease-modifying treatments that have come through late-stage trials in recent years, which target amyloid, the protein that builds up into plaques in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s. Dr. Sheona Scales, director of research at Alzheimer’s Research UK , called AR1001 “especially interesting” for that reason. “Rather than targeting amyloid, it acts on a specific enzyme and influences several other processes involved in brain function ,” she said. A tablet instead of an infusion The format matters too. Existing disease-modifying options require infusions or injections, while AR1001 is swallowed once a day. Dr. Richard Oakley, associate director of research and innovation at Alzheimer’s Society, said that difference “could make treatment simpler.” Phase 3 trial results in detail 13 countries, 604 key participants The phase 3 trial, known as Polaris-AD , enrolled patients with early Alzheimer’s across 13 countries, including the UK. The headline result comes from the 604 participants who were taking no other Alzheimer’s drugs, a group in which the decline in memory and thinking slowed by nearly a third compared with placebo. “Over the year of the trial, this drug was able to effectively slow down people’s decline in memory and thinking by nearly a third, and the side-effects reported were mostly mild to moderate,” Oakley said. The subgroup question The catch is in the wider group. Among patients who were also taking existing medications for Alzheimer’s symptoms, AR1001 did not produce a statistically significant benefit, which means the trial missed significance across its full population. Scales acknowledged as much. “The trial demonstrated a statistically significant slowing of clinical decline in participants who were not taking other commonly used Alzheimer’s medications alongside the trial drug. However, this benefit was not significant across the overall trial group,” she said. Oakley said the reason for that gap needs further investigation. Next steps for a new Alzheimer’s treatment Regulators and further trials None of the experts treated the results as final. All called for additional trials, and the findings still need review by independent scientists and drug regulators before AR1001 could be prescribed. Oakley also warned against improvising with existing drugs. “AR1001 is from the same family of medicines as Viagra, but it is being developed specifically for Alzheimer’s disease,” he said, adding that people should not take Viagra to try to treat the condition. A different route against dementia The stakes are large. Alzheimer’ s is the most common form of dementia, and dementia is forecast to affect 153 million people worldwide by 2050, with no cure available. Scales described the results as “an important milestone in the search for new Alzheimer’s treatments,” and Oakley said they were “an exciting sign that we could have a totally new treatment for early Alzheimer’s disease that tackles its causes, not just its symptoms.” If larger studies confirm the effect and explain why it disappeared in patients on other medications, a daily tablet working through blood flow would give doctors a second line of attack alongside the amyloid drugs. items.descriptionOriginal: Data from 10,000 workers show sit-stand desks boost active work time by 43 minutes a day—or roughly $9,000 in annual productivity per employee. Every workday is a negotiation between our bodies and our jobs. Sit too long, our backs and necks protest; stand too long, our feet might have something to say about it. Sit-stand desks, also known as height-adjustable desks or standing desks, promise a healthier way to work, giving employees the flexibility to alternate between sitting and standing throughout the day. Now, new research suggests these desks may be giving employees, and employers, another benefit beyond ergonomics and well-being: productivity. Drawing on data from more than 10,000 employees, researchers at Texas A&M University found that workers who used sit-stand desks averaged 43 additional minutes of active computer use each day compared with those using regular desks, a difference that could translate to nearly $9,000 in annual productivity per employee. The study, published in Theoretical and Applied Ergonomics , was co-led by Texas A&M School of Public Health professor Mark Benden and US Army Public Health Command Region, West, Regional Ergonomist Tricia Salzar. The findings suggest that the physical workspace may be a powerful, often overlooked, influence on employee well-being, productivity, and even a company’s overall performance. When organizations look to boost performance and productivity, they turn to new technologies, training programs and management strategies. But another powerful influence may be hiding in plain sight: the physical workplace itself. “It’s what we call the ‘workplace effect,'” Benden says. “The direct impact that the physical work environment has on the behavior, health, psychological well-being, and even engagement and performance of employees.” Sit-stand desks are a striking example of the workplace effect. Rather than locking employees into a single position for hours at a time, they give workers the flexibility to sit, stand and move throughout the day, as tasks and energy levels shift. “It can have a profound effect,” Benden says. “Alternating between different working positions promotes better health outcomes by reducing physical strain and encouraging movement for those who might otherwise spend most of their workday sedentary.” But the benefits may extend beyond physical health. Benden and Salzar’s new research shows that sit-stand desks can also have a substantial impact on productivity. “It has a cumulative, positive effect for both employers and employees,” Benden says. For employees, height-adjustable desks could lead to sustained energy and longer stretches of focused work. For employers, the higher work productivity could translate into a nearly $9,000 return on investment per employee annually. “The implications are hard to ignore,” Benden says. “When we design workplaces around employees and their needs, better health, better performance and better organizational outcomes follow.” The takeaway? Investing in the physical workplace, like height-adjustable desks, isn’t just good for employee comfort and health; it could be good for business, too. To test whether sit-stand desks could influence work output and productivity, Benden and his colleagues stepped out of their labs and turned to the real world, using a resource few ergonomics studies can match. “We analyzed a huge dataset of more than 10,000 workers over a yearlong period, comparing the total computer use of traditional desk users and height-adjustable desk users,” Benden says. The records paired employee comfort surveys with a digital trail of workplace activity, tracking everything from keystrokes and words typed to mouse clicks and typing errors, all to paint a detailed picture of how employees interacted with their computers throughout the workday. “It was important that we collected subjective measurements, like employee survey responses of their comfort and objective measurements of computer activity through software, to analyze how people engaged with their work,” Benden says. The team found that workers with sit-stand desks averaged 3.66 hours of active computer time, compared with 2.95 hours among regular-desk employees—a gap of about 43 minutes a day. That might not sound like much, but over a year it adds up to roughly 171 additional hours, or more than four 40-hour workweeks. And those additional hours come with a practical price tag, too. Multiplying the 171 additional hours by a standardized hourly wage of about $52, the researchers estimate that sit-stand desks could generate nearly $9,000 in potential annual productivity value per employee. “Our findings were exciting because they suggest that height-adjustable desks can directly influence overall work output and economic organizational productivity,” Benden says. The researchers also found that employees using sit-stand desks generally typed more words and logged more keystrokes than their counterparts at non-adjustable desks. “The data showed that people aren’t just engaging with their work, they are producing output in a meaningful way,” Benden says. For Benden, the findings open the door to broader questions about the future of organizations, focusing on another force rapidly reshaping the modern workplace. “Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly integrated into daily work,” Benden says. “Just as we’ve studied how the physical environment affects human health and performance, we’re interested in understanding how emerging AI technologies could influence the physical workspace and outcomes of organizations.” From adjustable desks to emerging technologies, the underlying question remains the same: how can organizations design environments and systems to better support the people who use them? “The next breakthrough may not come from working harder, but from designing workspaces and systems that help people work smarter and more efficiently,” Benden says. The story told by the more than 10,000 employees is that the desk may be doing far more than just holding up your computer. For Benden, sit-stand desks represent more than an ergonomic innovation. They’re part of a lifelong passion to understand how workplaces can be designed to better support employee well-being and organizational success. “We spend a lot of time at work,” Benden says. “It’s my passion to make sure that workers feel supported in their workplace, built on informed and guided scientific evidence.” A former Army Reserve officer, engineer, healthcare professional, inventor and world-renowned researcher, Benden has spent decades studying the complex relationship between people and the environments in which they work. So, the next time you find yourself slumping in your chair at 3pm with an aching back, don’t just reach for another cup of coffee, because the verdict is in: show this study to your boss. Your back—and your company’s bottom line—will thank you. Source: Texas A&M University The post Sit-stand desks boost active work time by 43 minutes a day appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: A s a taxi driver, Juan Barbosa should in theory be one of the strongest opponents of a crackdown on cars. But, puffing on a cigarette beside his vehicle on a sultry August afternoon, the inhabitant of Pontevedra, Spain, admits that he finds himself in something of an existential crisis. “As a driver, I suffer,” says Barbosa, who has been ferrying passengers around the northwestern city for two decades. “We can’t enter certain areas unless we have a customer or a booking. We have to take longer routes. But as a pedestrian, life is better. I enjoy it when there are fewer vehicles around.” Post-pandemic, pedestrian-first urban planning is now all the rage, from 15-minute cities to low-traffic zones and the rise of soft mobility ( human-powered or low-emission electric transport). But Pontevedra, which is home to 85,000 people in the city and just under a million in the province, was way ahead of the curve. It technically began its war on cars last century. (In 1999, to be precise.) The urban transformation of Pontevedra was carried out gradually, over the course of several years. Credit: Peter Yeung Today Pontevedra, which fittingly is located on one of the world-famous Camino de Santiago pilgrimage routes , is considered perhaps the greatest example in the world when it comes to getting rid of cars. Every year, delegations of mayors, professors and city planners make their own pilgrimage to learn about this great vanishing act. “Pontevedra is an influential example and something we speak of often,” says Mark Nieuwenhuijsen , director of the urban planning, environment and health initiative at ISGlobal, a public health research institute based in Barcelona. “Many cities are now following their direction: It reduces air pollution, noise, and livability improves.” Over the course of the 20th century, the city came to be dominated by vehicles. By the late 1990s, an average of 80,000 cars drove through Pontevedra every day — astonishingly, according to the municipality, three times more than through Madrid and five times more than London. Many of these vehicles weren’t even heading for the city, but rather transiting to other destinations such as beach towns on the coast. Those that did stay would turn the city’s charming historic squares into parking lots. Pontevedra before it was redesigned for pedestrians. Credit: Council of Pontevedra This came at a cost. Pontevedra’s epoch of cars dirtied the air, led to the deaths of pedestrians and seized centuries-old public spaces from residents. “The city was loud, disagreeable, unlivable,” says Miguel Anxo Fernández Lores, the longstanding mayor of Pontevedra, from the desk of his city hall office. “All the roads were filled with cars. The city was like a huge, permanent traffic jam.” Fernández Lores, a doctor by trade, decided enough was enough. In 1999, he campaigned to reclaim Pontevedra’s streets. The population agreed and elected him. Yet the urban transformation was not overnight. It has been carried out gradually. Fernández Lores began with a major effort to keep unnecessary cars out of the historic city center, removing significant amounts of on-street parking and only allowing essential vehicles to enter. Within one month in office, he had pedestrianized 300,000 square meters of the city center. In other parts of the city, he narrowed roads and widened sidewalks, introduced 30 kilometer per hour speed limits citywide, down from 50 kilometers per hour, and began installing traffic-calming measures like raised pedestrian crosswalks as well as almost 300 speed bumps. To take one example, the central Benito Corbel Street once had four lanes of traffic. In 2000, that was reduced to two lanes with widened sidewalks and trees. By 2014, it became a single-track road with only service vehicles able to enter, and even then for a limited time. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] The mayor, who passed a Traffic and Mobility Plan for Pontevedra in 2011 formalizing and defining his pedestrian-first approach, also developed infrastructure to make it easier to ditch cars. The city now has roughly 4,500 private underground parking spaces and about 3,500 free “park and ride” spaces, all within a short walking distance from the center. Traffic lights were replaced by roundabouts to facilitate the flow of the remaining vehicles. In some central areas, the speed limit was lowered to just 10 kilometers per hour. Trees, green spaces and street lighting were also added to improve livability. But despite its reputation, Pontevedra is not completely car-free — it allows certain vehicles on its streets within reason. “It’s not a city without cars,” says Fernández Lores. “But we only let the ones that really need to come here in.” Miguel Anxo Fernández Lores, the longstanding mayor of Pontevedra. Credit: Peter Yeung Residents can drive to garaged parking spots in the city. People with disabilities are free to drive in Pontevedra as long as they have a permit. And vehicles used for emergencies and public services such as garbage and water trucks and ambulances are permitted 24/7. Home deliveries, house moving and loading and unloading by businesses are allowed, but only during certain hours. And indeed, taxi drivers like Barbosa may enter certain zones if they have a client or booking. When necessary, police can issue fines of several hundred euros, ensuring these limits are respected. “I think it was very smart, the decisions they made,” says Mirian Calvo , a researcher and expert in urban design from Pontevedra. “And this philosophy, of mixed-traffic, prioritizing soft mobility, has been applied over 30 years, more or less.” The results of Pontevedra’s policy to prioritize pedestrians in public spaces, sustained over more than a quarter of a century, are nothing short of stunning. Car trips in the city center have fallen by 97 percent, according to official municipal figures. The air is markedly cleaner, with CO2 emissions dropping by about 70 percent. And the streets are much safer: There have been no traffic deaths since 2011, whereas between 1996 and 2006, 30 people died in traffic accidents. (Pontevedra has won European road safety awards in the process.) The streets of Pontevedra have gotten much safer: There have been no traffic deaths since 2011. Credit: Pilar Picas / Shutterstock In fact, about 90 percent of all journeys in the city center are by foot, with road safety so high that 80 percent of kids aged 6 to 12 walk without their parents to school each morning. Many local business owners have signed up to be supervisors if the children need help for any reason. For all the talk of the climate and safety benefits that come with limiting vehicle traffic and designing pedestrian-first urban spaces, however, there has been a surprising further advantage: Pontevedra is thriving economically. While in the 1990s, retail activity was drifting towards the suburbs, the decision to prioritize a compact, walkable city with a high quality of life, has changed the picture drastically. The mayor, for his part, has rejected proposals to build malls on the urban periphery, protecting the pedestrian-oriented urban core. “We don’t want huge malls, we want small, independent businesses,” says Fernández Lores. Pontevedra is now the fastest-growing city in the region of Galicia and in recent years has attracted 15,000 new inhabitants, mostly young families from elsewhere in northwest Spain. It also generates more jobs per capita than any other city in the region. The results of Pontevedra’s policy to prioritize pedestrians in public spaces, sustained over more than a quarter of a century, are nothing short of stunning. Credit: Peter Yeung “It’s a very convenient city now,” says Calvo. “It’s a very nice city to live in and people can see that.” Most locals are effusive in their praise. Esther Louzao, 68, says that her home near Plaza Pelegrina was once surrounded by cars, but not anymore. She has even stopped driving to work, instead opting to go by bus. But she keeps her car for beach days. “I like it a lot, it’s easier to walk,” says Louzao, fittingly waiting at a bus stop. Pacing down the street with a stroller, Anna, a 39-year-old with a toddler son who lives four kilometers out of town, agrees. “It’s better, much safer, it’s pleasant,” she explains. “Even if sometimes my journeys take a bit longer.” Yet not all residents are entirely convinced by the policy. Manuel, who has been living in Pontevedra for 40 years, believes the transformation has been overstated. He owns three cars: one for the city, one for going to the beach and a third for sport driving. “Yes, the city is a lot different to how it was before,” says Manuel. “But it’s not as perfect as it seems. Some of us still need cars.” In Spain, all municipalities with over 50,000 inhabitants are now required have a low emission zone, like this one in Santander. Credit: Scharfsinn / Shutterstock Calvo agrees, noting that Pontevedra’s public transit network is lacking, which means that elderly people suffer and that cars must be taken to the coastal beaches. A system like Rome’s fleet of electric minibuses in the historic center could be implemented, she says. And although the results of Pontevedra’s policy are hard to deny, Calvo, who is also a lecturer in participatory architecture, argues that the system could have been even more effective and popular if residents had been more involved in the process. In the 2000s, she says, there was significant opposition to the project, even if that has now disappeared due to the clearly positive impact. “I don’t think there has been serious public engagement,” she says. “There are more things that could be done to make it more participatory.” Nieuwenhuijsen, however, commends Pontevedra’s less confrontational approach, which presented the restriction of cars as about livability. “I think everyone would prefer places with less noise and less pollution,” he says. “It shouldn’t be about the war on cars, presented as punishing someone.” In 2019, Oslo became the first European capital to effectively make its city center car-free. Credit: OlgaVysh / Shutterstock In any case, cities across the world are following in Pontevedra’s pioneering footsteps. In 2019, Oslo became the first European capital to effectively make its city center car-free by removing on-street parking spaces and restricting access. Freiburg, Germany, has similarly transformed the district of Vauban into a car-free zone, banning on-street parking and introducing vehicle speed limits at walking pace on residential streets. And in 2022, the Spanish government approved a royal decree requiring all municipalities with over 50,000 inhabitants to have a low emission zone, and recommending the use of traffic-restricted areas like that of Pontevedra. Yet not every place can easily replicate Pontevedra’s success. Professor Nieuwenhuijsen admits the transformation of North American cities could be more challenging given their size and lack of density. “U.S. cities were built around the car,” he says. “You get a lot of sprawl. European cities are different, many were designed for walking and horse carriages.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Likewise, transforming larger cities will not be as easy. Redesigning urban areas could be slowed or halted by infrastructure such as underground piping, adds Nieuwenhuijsen, and the investment required could prove prohibitive. Barcelona’s Superblocks cost as little as €500,000 but as much as €10 million per unit in some cases. But Fernández Lores, who is planning to run for an eighth term in 2027, believes that bigger cities could begin shifting away from cars and towards pedestrians by focusing on districts rather than entire cities. A case in point: In 2023, Culdesac Tempe, Arizona, became the first purpose-built, entirely car-free residential neighborhood in the U.S. “Cities work without cars,” he says. “But each city must find its own way.” The post The City That Kicked Out Cars Before It Was Cool appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s a particular feeling that comes with lifting the lid off the holiday storage bin. The tangle of lights, the ornament with the chipped corner, the little ceramic village you’ve set up on the same shelf for as long as you can remember. It’s comforting, and there’s a reason traditions stick around. But somewhere around the third box, the comfort can start to tip into a sort of déjà vu, and you might catch yourself wondering whether it’s time to start over. Before you head to the store, though, try a different idea. The holiday decorations you already own can look surprisingly different with a little rearranging, a few things from outside, and a willingness to break your own habits. Here are six ways to do it, whether you’re decking the halls for Thanksgiving , Christmas, Hanukkah or all of the above. Rethinking where holiday decorations go Give every piece a new home Most of us decorate on autopilot. The wreath goes on the same hook, the nativity scene lands on the same bookshelf, and the whole house ends up looking exactly like it did last year, because it is exactly like last year. This time, pause before you put anything down. Hold each piece and ask where else it could live. That nativity scene might feel brand new on the entryway table, where it’s the first thing people see. If you’re stuck, give yourself a rule: everything that usually goes upstairs goes downstairs this year, and vice versa. Choose one theme and edit to fit it Instead of pulling out every decoration you own, pick a theme and use only what matches. It can be as simple as one color, like all greens, or one motif, like snowflakes or anything that sparkles. Leaving some favorites in the box for a year can make them feel special again when they come back out, and the pieces you do use will look more intentional together. Bringing in natural and handmade touches Decorate with what’s growing outside Your backyard or a neighborhood walk can fill in a lot of gaps at no cost. A handful of pinecones lined along the mantel, or a few bare branches standing tall in a big vase on the kitchen island, adds texture and makes the familiar pieces around them look fresher. Dried citrus is another easy one. Slice oranges or grapefruit thin, dry them in a low oven until they turn translucent, and string them into a garland. Any extra slices make a lovely garnish for a winter drink. Add something your family made Handmade decorations carry a warmth store-bought ones can’t match. You could decide that this is the year the tree only gets ornaments made at the kitchen table, or have everyone in the house paint their own candle for the menorah. The pieces don’t need to be perfect. The slightly lopsided ones tend to become the favorites. Small changes to familiar holiday decor Trade your lights around String lights are easy to move, so let them wander. Bring the indoor lights outside and the outdoor ones in, or take the strand that usually wraps the tree and frame a doorway with it instead. Before anything goes outside, check that it’s rated for outdoor use, since indoor lights left out in the weather can become a fire hazard. Paint, mix and remake If you’re truly tired of a piece, change how it looks. Spray paint a set of old ornaments in a new color, hand-paint plain candles, or combine figures from two or three mismatched nativity sets into one scene. Experimenting is low-risk here. If you end up disliking the result, you were already ready to retire it, and if you love it, you’ve got something that feels new without buying a single thing, which might be the nicest kind of holiday surprise there is. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Women in England and Wales who were arrested, cautioned or convicted for ending their own pregnancies no longer carry those records. Automatic abortion pardons took effect on November 16, and police and courts must now delete the details of past convictions, cautions, arrests and investigations wherever they can. The women affected don’t need to apply, pay a fee, or contact anyone. The pardons come under Section 242 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026 , passed earlier this year alongside a separate provision that removed women from criminal law for ending their own pregnancies. Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, who brought forward the decriminalization amendment, says the change will clear the names of more than 100 women who were “unnecessarily harmed” by an “outdated” law. How the abortion pardons work Records deleted, or treated as deleted The pardon applies to abortion offenses relating to a woman’s own pregnancy, including cases where she acted beyond the legal time limits. Where full deletion from police and court systems isn’t possible, records must be marked so they are treated as erased. Alex Davies-Jones, the minister for victims and tackling violence against women and girls , said the pardons had been a priority. “Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team,” she said. What remains illegal The change ends prosecution of women over their own pregnancies, but abortion itself is still regulated. In England and Wales, abortion with an authorized provider is legal up to 24 weeks, with narrow exceptions after that point, such as when the mother’s life is at risk or the baby would be born with a severe disability. Medication taken at home is permitted before 10 weeks. Doctors and anyone else who act outside the Abortion Act 1967 can still face charges. Ending a Victorian law’s reach Nicola Packer’s five-year ordeal The law that the change dismantles dates to 1861, and the cases brought under it in recent years show what it meant in practice. In 2020, during a Covid lockdown, Nicola Packer, then 41, was prescribed abortion medication by phone through the National Health Service. She believed she was a few weeks pregnant. In fact, she was around 26 weeks along. Her friend Helle Tumbridge, speaking to the BBC with Packer’s consent, said she had experienced what’s known as a cryptic pregnancy. “That’s when you don’t have any sign of a pregnancy, no baby bump, no other symptoms,” she said. After a stillbirth, Packer went to the hospital, and staff called the police. “She was arrested. She spent a time in her hospital room recovering with two police officers present, one was a man. She was treated appallingly,” Tumbridge said. It took five years of investigation before a jury unanimously cleared her. “Of course, by that point the damage had been done, and she’ll live with that trauma for the rest of her life,” Tumbridge said. The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists said at the time that her trial showed “just how outdated and harmful” the law was. Reactions to the pardons Providers and advocates Heidi Stewart of the abortion care provider BPAS acknowledged that a pardon has limits. “While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice,” she said. Opponents of decriminalization Not everyone sees the change that way. Anti-abortion groups opposed both decriminalization and the pardons, arguing that removing criminal penalties, including for abortions late in pregnancy, leaves the unborn without legal protection. John Deighan, CEO of the Society for the Protection of Unborn Children, said in April that the pardons law “disgraces the children who have been needlessly destroyed in the past.” For the women whose records are now being cleared, the practical effect will show up in background checks, job applications, and travel paperwork that no longer carry a conviction or arrest. Antoniazzi and other supporters will be watching how smoothly police and courts carry out the deletions in the months ahead, since the pardon only works if the paperwork follows.
